Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 86, to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This Bill is introduced at the instance of the Ontario Government. They have by recent legislation modified their system of reformatories, more particularly by establishing institutions known as industrial farms, and the principal purpose of this Bill is to make applicable to those industrial farms the provisions of the Prisons and Reformatories Act. Provision is also made in this Bill for the transfer of prisoners from the jails to the industrial farms. Another provision gives wider powers than they have hitherto enjoyed to the Parole Board, which was established in connection with the reformatories by the Lieutenant-Governor of Ontario, these powers being with regard to the determination or suspension of indeterminate sentences.
A good idea.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: The House again in Committee on Bill No. 66, in aid of provincial legislation prohibiting or restricting the sale or use of intoxicating liquors-Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice); Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
When the Bill was last considered in committee, a motion was under consideration, which was moved by the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) as an addition to the Bill. Before we deal with that, if I may be permitted, I should like to refer to suggestions made, one by the hon. member for Queens, P.E.I. (Mr. A. A. McLean) and the other by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) supported, I think, by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). Upon consideration, I am inclined to think there was more in what was pointed out than, on the spur of the moment, I was disposed to believe. I am not prepared to say that amendment of the section is really necessitated .by what was said, but I am quite prepared to concede that there is more than enough in it to make it wise that I should act upon both these suggestions. I am referring, if I have the permission of the committee, to section 1. The suggestion of the hon. member for Queens, P.E.I., was that the wording of the Bill:	"Any person who, by himself, his
clerk, servant, or agent," might be interpreted to exclude responsibility on the part ol the clerk or agent. As I say, I am not prepared to accept that view, but I do want to avoid any difficulty about interpretation. The other suggestion, in which, I say quite frankly, I Think there is much more than in the first I have mentioned, was that of the hon. member for St. John. In the view of that hon. gentleman the manager, agents, or employees of a govem-railway would not be subject to prosecution under this Act if they carried liquor

in violation of the Act. While I am not ready to say that I absolutely adopt that view, I am still free to concede that the positive view I entertained upon the subject was, perhaps, not justified, and that possibly there is room for the section being interpreted in the way the hon. member for St. John suggested. While I still believe that what I said is correct, speaking as a general proposition, I think now that I did not give sufficient attention to the fact that the unlawfulness of things done in violation of the Act would be the result of this Act alone, and that the view might be entertained that, the Crown not being specified by this Act, that which was done by a Government railway not otherwise unlawful, would -not come within the purview of this Act If I am permitted, I would move that section 1 be reconsidered.

Motion agreed to.

speechtext:
I appreciate the difficulty of dealing with the subject of carrying within the province on Government railways. The question is whether or not a provincial legislature could pass a law which would impose any penalty upon the Crown as represented by the Dominion Government or its employees. The minister is aware, of course, that the courts of th.e country have determined that employees of the Dominion Government cannot be taxed by the provincial legislatures, on the ground that if that could toe done it would be giving the provincial legislatures authority to hamper, in seme way, the administration of public affairs by the Dominion Government. I have never been able to see the reasonableness of that. I have always thought it was taking a very narrow view. But still the courts have held that, and the consequence is that to-day, throughout Canada, the officials of the Dominion Government are not taxed by the various muni-

cipalities. I know that was the decision of the Supreme Court of New Brunswick, and 1 think it was upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada. If that is good law-and, of course, we are bound to assume that any decision, once made, is good law-I should think it would follow, as a matter of course, that the provincial governments could not impose penalties upon the employees of the Dominion Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.

speechtext:
I am disposed to think that the hon. gentleman's view is correct, but we are dealing with a Bill that has to do with the transportation of goods from one province into another.. I think we may, for the moment, leave aside the Intercolonial and its peculiar situation, and we may say that it is quite within the purview of a province to make legislation as to the carriage of goods within the province. I agree that such provincial legislation would not, of its own force, apply to the Intercolonial, but I think a more proper place to deal with, that question, as affecting the Intercolonial railway, would be in connection with the Acts concerning the Government railways. If a province made a law of application to carriers generally in that province in regard to the transportation of liquor, it would be a proper thing that the Intercolonial should be made subject to that law; and if I am in a position to do it, when that action is taken toy any province, I will be very glad to help to supplement it 'by legislation of this Parliament. But in the meantime this hardly seems to be the proper place in which to interject a provision of that sort.
Section as amended agreed to.
On the proposed amendment of Mr. Stevens, to add the following to section 2 of the Bill:
In addition to any other penalties prescribed for a violation of section one of this Act, any person holding a license to carry on the business or trade of a distiller or brewer, issued under the provisions of the Inland Revenue Act, who violates the provisions of section one of this Act, or who sells or delivers intoxicating liquor in violation of the law in force in any province, shall also be liable in any prosecution under this Act, on conviction for a first offence, to the suspension of such license for any" period not exceeding three months, and on conviction for a second offence, to the suspension of his license for any period not exceeding six months, and on conviction for a third offence, shall forfeit his license and shall thereafter be unable to hold such a license.

Mr- HUGHES: I agree with the minister that a good time to impose conditions would be when the subsidies are being granted.

speechtext: After looking carefully at the wording of the amendment proposed, I find that while it fs intended to impose suspension or cancellation of a license as a consequence not only of violations of- this proposed Act but of violations of the provisions of any Provincial Act, the section, as drawn, indicates that the liability shall be incurred " in any prosecution under this Act." If he is simply selling liquor within a province which has a law forbidding the sale within that province, he will be violating the law of the province, but it is intended to attach to his conviction a can- cellation or suspension not only for the violation of this Act but for the violation on the part of the licensee of the Dominion of a Provincial Act.

subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Of course, a prosecution for violating a Provincial Act will naturally

be taken in the provincial courts. In a subsequent provision of this Act we provide that a man violating this Act may be prosecuted either at the place whence he . sends this liquor or at the place to which h he sends the liquor. The place to which he sends the liquor will be within a prohibitory province, so that if he is a man in an outside province, he may be prosecuted before the courts of the province into which he has sent the liquor in violation of the law of that province.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Being a layman, perhaps I do not understand the legal significance of the matter. The hon. gentleman has referred to the fact that an alleged violator of the law may be prosecuted either in the province to which the liquor has gone or in the province from which it is sent. Would it be possible for him to be prosecuted in both provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
If he was convicted in one place he would have a perfect defence in another province in that he had been once convicted. He is only guilty of one offence. Under the general pro-4 p.m. visions of the law he is protected against being tried or convicted in two places. There are under the general law-provisions in which, under certain circumstances, a man can be tried at one place or at another. For instance, a man who is prosecuted for criminal libel can be prosecuted in the place where the libel was circulated. Although he may publish his paper in one province, if the libellous matter is circulated in another province, he may be sued in another province. Of course, he can be sued in his own province, but he could not be prosecuted by reason of the same offence
Mr. GRAHAM. If a man were charged with having sent liquor into this province, say, and a prosecution took place in Ontario, would it be possible, if he should be acquitted in Ontario, that he might still be prosecuted in Quebec for sending it in if they had not proved that it had reached its destination in Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I do not think so. The offence is one and the same, and I think he would have a perfect defence in that he had once been put upon his trial and acquitted. I think it would be just as good a defence if he had been convicted.

subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: You are making it worse now.

subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The law can be evaded, and much more easily evaded toy reason of the failure of the Minister of Justice to provide for a public prosecutor. He must see how easy it would be for the distillers to escape punishment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: We have guarded against that by imposing a minimum penalty; so even an easy-going, friendly magistrate could not fine an offender less than $100.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: What is $100?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
That is for the first offence. When it comes to the third offence the magistrate has no option but to send the offender to jail. With, regard to the risks of a friendly magistrate entering into collusion with a man of this kind, those are the risks we have to run in the application of the law generally. Even where a man is susceptible of prosecution in any one place, there are different magistrates, different stipendary magistrates, and different officers, and if we are going to begin to provide against what verges on corruption of the magistracy we shall have to provide against that in the application of other laws as well as in this particular one. It seems to me we have afforded adequate protection. I have already said what I hav? to say on the question of the appointment of a public prosecutor. The whole system of our law proceeds upon the assumption that the administration and the enforcement of the law belongs to the province.

We are willing to leave the enforcement of the provisions of our Criminal Code, so far as any Government is charged with their enforcement, in the hands of the province; and if there be any law that may safely be left to the provinces to enforce, it would seem to he a law which is provided for the specific purpose of rendering more effective the province's own law. This law is intended to make effective the laws of provinces that desire prohibition; we are handing to those provinces an instrument to make their law more effective. Now, if we can trust the provinces generally to enforce our criminal law, it would seem to me that we might in a very special manner rely upon a province to see to the enforcement of this law, which is enacted for the precise purpose of enabling them to make their own law more effective.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Many years ago a great many people had the same faith in the ease with which prohibitory laws could be enforced. The Minister of Trade and Commerce remembers what enthusiasm existed a great many years ago in New Brunswick in connection with the enforcement of the Canada Temperance Act; but, somehow, lawyers iseem to be able to display much more ingenuity in driving a horse and cart through a prohibitory law than through any otherv kind of law placed upon the statute book. Difficulties which one could never have conceived of have arisen in connection with the enforcement of the Canada Temperance Act, and the result has been that year after year Parliament has made amendments which, I am sure, Parliament would never have thought of making in connection with'any other law upon the statute book. For instance, Parliament had to enact that the right of search should be taken away, and that there should be no appeal from a magistrate's decision if there was no evidence of the guilt of the accused.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Would you suggest that a clause be put in the Act to the effect that this Act 'shall prohibit, notwithstanding anything else that may appear in the statute book?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
That is what is intended, of course. The difficulty is that the minister, while impressed with the idea that this Parliament should give the provinces an instrument, as he calls it, to enable them better to carry out their wishes, is really not giving them an effective instrument at all. The reason for this law is that liquor is brought in from outside and
distributed in provinces where prohibition is in force, and whose people are desirous of keeping prohibition in force. For instance, a violation of the prohibitory law of Prince Edward Island may have its origin in a distant part of the Dominion, perhaps a thousand miles away. The minister makes no provision for enforcing the law against the distillers in that distant province, but throws the burden on the people of the prohibition province, who, as I said, may be a thousand miles from where the offence originated; and the temperance people, who, after all, you have to rely on to enforce the law, could not go to the expense of employing lawyers and meeting all the difficulties which lawyers for the defense would bring against them, in a case so far from home. This Government has the duty of enforcing the law of Canada, and I say it should bear the burden in respect of offences committed outside of a province that is directly interested. There is no question about that. Just think of the difficulties that might arise in respect of a conviction, and the taking away of a distiller's license! The minister has very properly stated that a -man cannot 'be tried twice for the same offence. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) was going to suggest that that right was included in the Magna Charts, but being a layman he did not care to do so. But there is no doubt that that is the case. This Bill provides that on a third offence a distiller's license shall be taken away. But the minister knows that that result would not happen unless the information that was laid declared it to be a third offence. Unless the information and all the proceedings declare that it is a second or a third offence, as the case may be, the Taw in every instance regards it as a first offence, and unless there is in the province where the offence originated somebody directly interested in the enforcement of the law, so far as it affects the province immediately concerned, the distiller would simply be fined for an offence that would not cause a cancellation of his license. For instance, when proceedings came to be taken in Prince Edward Island, let us say, a conviction in Ontario would be set up, and the distiller would ibe discharged as having already been fined. Unless you have somebody to watch those proceedings and see that they are properly carried on, I am satisfied that the law, so far as its enforcement is concerned, will

be simply a farce. An honest effort was made in the different provinces of Canada to enforce the Canada Temperance Act, but there was great difficulty in enforcing it owing to the numerous objections and the doubts which were raised as to what the various sections meant, and those objections and doubts really made the Canada Temperance Act a farce, so far as enforcement was concerned, in some of the provinces, and possibly in all. I think it is on account of the difficulty in enforcing the law that the demand has come for provincial and Dominion-wide prohibition.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Does not venue lie in both places? That is to say, if people wish to prosecute in either province, can they not do so?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Under this Bill, prosecution may be made in either province.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: What has that to do with prosecution a thousand miles away?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I will tell my hon. friend one difficulty. Suppose a prosecution takes place in Prince Edward Island for a violation there; the offender may be in Ontario, one thousand miles away, and be has to be served with a process. I doubt very much if the process of a Prince Edward . Island magistrate would run into Ontario unless you had some special provision in the Bill which would enable a distiller to be served in Ontario. If a distiller having his business in Ontario were fined in Prince Edward Island, I am not quite sure how the penalty could be collected. The distiller has no place of business, no residence, no goods and chattels in Prince Edward Island upon which a levy can be made. How is the penalty to be enforced? Are the temperance people of Prince Edward Island to go into Ontario in order' to endeavour to enforce a conviction? I doubt very much whether they can do so. As my hon. friend takes enough interest in this matter to ask questions, I would be glad if he would apply his intellect to this question and find out some means (by which this law could be enforced. If there is an honest desire to make this an effective means of enforcing provincial prohibition there is only one way to do it, namely, to provide officers who, under the instructions of the Department of Justice, will enforce tb.e law in the province where the offence originated, and not compel the people of the far-off province, where the offence is consummated, to go long distances at great expense in order to obtain a conviction.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Would not the
person who carried the liquor into the province be liable in the province? Would not that be a separate prosecution? Would not the person who sent the liquor, say, from Ontario to Nova Scotia, also be liable? Would not the person who carried the goods and also the person who sent them be liable?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I was dealing with the question of proceedings against the distiller. It has been thought by the Minister of Justice that it will make the Bill more effective to enable the manufacturer, or distiller, to be proceeded against by reason of his sending his goods by steamship or railway into a province which is prohibited territory. I think myself that, if proceedings can be taken against a manufacturer, the law can be much more easily enforced. What I was speaking of was the fact that there is no clear nor effective method provided by this Bill of enforcing the law as against the manufacturer who may be outside of the province directly interested, and, as I have said, may be not only hundreds of miles, but one or two thousand miles away.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
May I suggest to the
minister, as this Bill seems to be very complicated, that the easiest thing to do is to withdraw it and bring in a simple Bill prohibiting the importation and manufacture of spirituous liquors for beverage purposes?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: In a word.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Just a short Bill. In that way you will get over all this complication.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I want to follow up for a moment the proposal of my hon. friend from St. John. I drew this matter to the attention of the minister when we were last discussing this Bill, and I regard it as really the most important matfeT in connection with the Bill. If the Fereral Government will undertake the task of enforcing the law outsde of the province where the legislature of the provonce prohibits, it will make the Bill effective. If they fail to do so, I fear that the Bill will not be effective. We have the experience of the Bill of 1908, which was similar to this in language and passed for a similar purpose, to prevent intoxicating liquor from being brought into and sold in counties that had adopted the Scott Act. At that time the counties of Nova Scotia, with the exception of one or two, had adopted the Scott Act, and it was regarded as very important to

have a measure of this kind that "would enable us to prosecute a merchant outside of the dry area for sending liquor into that area, and we secured that measure in 1908. It was, however, almost a dead letter on account of the fact that there was no method of prosecuting the man in the outside province who sent the liquor into the area covered by the Scott Act. This is not a new proposal for this Government. There are on the statute-book a number of very important Acts in connection with which the Department of Justice is dealing with prosecutions at the present time. Take, for instance, the' Fisheries Act. If a violation of that Act occurs along the coast, the Minister of Justice is notified and he has his organization to deal with it. He prosecutes the poacher, the man who violates the regulations in regard to fisheries. That is a duty that devolves upon the Department of Justice, and it carries out that work successfully throughout Canada. The same is true with regard to Inland Revenue. If a breach of the Inland Revenue regulations takes place in any province in Canada, the prosecution is dealt with by the Department of Justice and dealt -with successfully. The Weights and Measures Act is another statute in regard to which the Department of Justice deals with any violation of it. I understand that the proposal of my hon. friend from St. John is to adopt a somewhat similar principle in the Bill under discussion. If the minister will agree to adopt that principle, I think the measure will be a very successful one. Of course, he can see that at the present time each province can deal with offenders within its own boundaries. The provinces are not asking for any assistance from this Government to prosceute men who violate the provincial laws; but it a different matter entirely when the provincial authorities have to deal with a violation in a distant province. When I mentioned the matter to the minister the other day, he said: All you have to do is to lay an information in the province in which the violation is committed. That is to say, if a merchant in Montreal violates this law by sending liquor into Guysborough, the shire town of the county I represent, some person from that town will have to go to Montreal, lay an information there before a magistrate, employ solicitors and counsel there, and carry on a prosecution before the courts in Montreal, in order to punish the violator of this statute. The minister has the machinery
for the enforcement of this law; he has his officers and representative of the Department of Justice all over Canada, and it is the easiest thing in the world for him to take charge of these prosecutions, whereas, it is practically impossible that it could be done by the local authorities. I have a draft section here which I wish to submit to the minister for his consideration:
When an offence against the law of any province of Canada prohibiting or restricting the sale of injtoxicating liquor, or against the provisions of this Act, has been committed outside the boundaries of such province, it shall be the duty of the Department of Justice to take such steps as may be necessary to prosecute the party guilty of such offence.
If the minister will insert such a section, I think we will all give him credit for giving a Bill that will promote temperance in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
In the first place, this amendment asks that we should prosecute, not only for violation of this Act, but foT violation of a provincial law outside the province. I cannot conceive how there can be a violation of provincial law outside the province, because the provincial law runs only within the province. Nor can I see any good purpose in my repeating what I said the other evening: that there is nothing about this law that makes it any more necessary foi this Government to enforce it than there is about the laws generally.	The hon. member has pointed
out certain laws that he says we enforce,	as,	for instance, the Inland
Revenue Act and the . Customs Act. But these are for the collection of debts due to the Dominion, and we act in these cases as any man would act in connection with offences that affect him in his business. The general administration of the criminal law is in the hands of the province. It does seem to me that the provinces ought to be trusted to enforce this law. The hon. gentleman keeps repeating-because it is not the first time he has said it- that, if a sale is made in Montreal of goods delivered in violation of this Act in Ontario, a man will have to go. down to Montreal, employ lawyers and carry on a prosecution, and this, in the face of the express provision of this Bill that he may prosecute that man in Toronto, in the very province into which the liquor has been' brought. I do not know that I shall gain anything by repeating that. I have said it several times, and the hon. gentleman still says that the man who wished to prosecute will have to go to Montreal.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
How is the minister
going to get the witnesses to the shipping of the liquor in Toronto, or, say, in Nova Scotia? The witnesess must be called. The issuing of a summons in the city of Halifax to prosecute a man in Montreal for shipping the liquor through Halifax can have no force unless proof is produced.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: You will have to bring your witnesses.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Does the minister say
that witnesses must be subpoenaed in Montreal to go to Halifax to prove the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
You will have your
-choice of doing it in whatever way you find most convenient. If the statement is made that you must go to Montreal to prosecute, I say that, under this Act, that is not correct.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The minister says that the provinces are charged with the enforcement of the criminal law. That is true, speaking in a general sense, but there are exceptions. The Dominion Government has recognized in many cases its duty to enforce the criminal law. In a case of robbing the mails, or stealing money from a post office, the Postmaster General, through the Minister of Justice, will prosecute. Some years ago, when I was Attorney General of New Brunswick, I knew of a number of such cases in which the Dominion Government prosecuted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: When the Dominion Government's property is stolen it lays an information like any one else, and sets the law in motion against the offender.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
But they have their own, counsel to represent them at the trial. After obtaining the commitment they do not hand over the action to the provincial authorities, but carry the prosecution through. Here is the distinction-a distinction I had hoped to impress upon the minister, but apparently am not able to; the provinces have to do with the administration of the criminal law within the boundaries of the province, but the minister has provided here that a liquor dealer or liquor manufacturer, who sends liquor Into a province where a provincial prohibitory law is in force, shall be guilty of an offence. Take the case of the man in Montreal who sends liquor from Montreal to Prince Edward Island. That offence is not committed in Prince Edward Island. It is true, the minister, by his Bill, provides that the case
[Mr. Doherty. 1
may be tried, in Prince Edward Island, but the offence is committed jn the province of Quebec, and the minister has provided that the authorities of Prince Edward Islandtaking that province as an illustration

shall have cast upon them the duty of enforcing the law in the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Or the authorities in Quebec.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Does the hon. minister think for a moment that the authorities in any province are going to proceed against a distiller or wholesaler who may foe doing a perfectly lawful business in that province, and whose offence is really committed against the spirit of the law of the province into which the liquor finds its destination? It is absurd to suppose that the authorities of Ontario, for instance, are going to prosecute a distiller who is manufacturing, it may be, quite legally in Ontario, and whose offence really is that he has sent liquor to Prince Edward Island, or New Brunswick, or Nova Scotia, or some other distant province. It is casting an undue burden upon the provincial authorities to require them to go into another province for the purpose of prosecuting a distiller in such case as I have mentioned.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: If the hon. member for St. John were criminally libelled by a newspaper in Vancouver, would he allow the operator of that newspaper to snap his fingers at him, or pay no attention to him, or would he go to Vancouver and prosecute there?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: That is a different matter; that is a criminal offence which is committed in Vancouver. But here the offence is consummated by the liquor being received in the prohibited territory. The minister is providing that, instead of enforcing the law in the place where the offence is consummated, proceedings may be taken in the province where the offence originates. What I submit is that if this Government is sincerely desirous of strengthening the hands of the provincial authorities and of preventing violations of provincial prohibitory laws, it should take upon itself the burden of enforcing this law, at all events in respect to proceedings which are to be taken outside of the province immediately affected.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
In order to enforce the present laws, throughout the Dominion of Canada it is found necessary to appoint magistrates and constables in every village,

township, town and city, a very large number indeed. Do I understand the hon. gentleman to suggest that the Dominion Government by legislation that it may pass here should duplicate these officers all over Canada?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Not at all, it would not be necessary. All I ask is that the Dominion Government shall make it its business to eee that this law is enforced, not the provincial, laws. Let the provinces enforce their own laws; but for any violation of this law, in respect of which proceedings may be taken either in the province where the offence .is consummated by the receipt of the liquor or in the province where the offence originates by the liquor being shipped, the Dominion should proceed.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Would this not necessitate the appointment of new officials?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
No, no new officials would have to be appointed. Suppose a manufacturer, a distiller or brewer, in Quebec sends liquor to Prince Edward Island, where there is a prohibitory law now in force; under this law the distiller may be procedeed against in the province of Quebec. Ali that would be necessary would be for the prosecutor appointed by the Dominion Government to take proceedings before any one of the magistrates in the province of Quebec, submit the evidence showing the offence, and obtain a conviction. What I protest against is that the temperance people away down in Prince Edward Island or in any part of the Maritime Provinces, or out in Saskatchewan, perhaps in the Peace river district, or any other remote section to which liquor is sent from leading wholesale and manufacturing centres of Canada, should be put to the enormous expense of coming to the wholesale and manufacturing centres of Canada to prosecute offenders, and we know * that the most effectual prosecutions will be against the distillers, wholesale dealers and brewers, and the most effectual way to carry on prosecutions will be to have them in these leading centres, instead of in the provinces where the offences are consummated. If the minister is content to say that this Government is discharging its full duty to the temperance sentiment of this country by simply placing a law upon the statute book and not preparing to spend one single dollar in the enforcement of that law, let him take that position But surely this Government has a higher duty than simply to put a law upon the
statute book. It has the duty of seeing to the enforcement of that law, and there is no power in this country which can so effectually or so well enforce the law as the Dominion Government. The distillers, wholesale dealers, and brewers, in the leading centres are shipping their goods to all parts of this country. You may have a prohibitory law in every province, extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and you will find, as we know by experience,- as the people of Prince EdwaTd Island know by experience during the time they have had a prohibitory law,-that these distillers and brewers and wholesale dealers secretly shipping liquor to all parts of this country. Then, if instead of the local authorities being obliged to come to these leading centres to follow up these offences and secure evidence against the wholesale dealers and manufacturers who were originating these unlawful transactions, this Dominion Government were to have a few prosecutors, one in each of the leading centres, to carry on the necessary detective work, they could easily enforce the law with a comparatively smail expense. They would thus be able effectively to prevent violations of the Act, which this Parliament is now asked to place upon the statute book.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Ontario has those officials now-and I have no doubt that other provinces also have such officials-who are paid by the province to detect such offences.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Ontario has officials, but not officials to go into the province of Quebec.	[DOT]

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The province of Quebec has them too.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The province of Quebec is not interested in punishing people who send liquor to the province of Prince Edward Island.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
There must be some
good temperance people in Quebec.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Yes, what becomes oi your general temperance sentiment?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
That is quite true, there are good temperance people; but they are interested in seeing that liquor is not sold to communities in the province of Quebec where there is prohibition. Most of the people in one province do not care how much liquor is sent into some other province, but they do not want the law violated right in their own home. The Minis-



ter of Justice intimates that this Government does not enforce the criminal law. Then what is all this Dominion Police force? Do they not enforce the law against the white slave traffic? Why do they do that? Why do they not leave that to the provincial authorities? Surely the minister cannot put up the plea that they are interested in that in any financial way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
We are interested in
looking after the immigation coming to this country, which is purely our affair.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: It is not limited to immigration; it is within the purview of the law against the white slave traffic that the law shall be enforced in respect of women who are already in this country. It is not limited to immigrants.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The Dominion police do not look after violations of these laws in the country generally: We did have a little special vote to enable them to afford protection in that regard in connection with immigrants coming into this country.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The minister now says something that will be a surprise' to members of this House. When we were asked to vote $10,000 a year for the Dominion police to endeavour to suppress the wnite slave traffic, so-called, it was clearly understood that it was not limited to immigrants who might be brought into Canada; the money was intended to enforce the law generally, to prevent that illegal and deplorable traffic. And so I might mention many other instances, all going to show that if the minister wants to do this, he can do it. If this Government desires to enforce this law, it has the machinery, it has the detectives, it can easily utilize its Dominion police. It could appoint a few public prosecutors, whose duty, it would be to take the necessary steps to enforce the law, and then this Act could be effectively enforced: As I have said before, if this Government feels that it has no interest at all in the suppression of intemperance in this country, that its whole duty is discharged when it simply puts in black and white the Jaw, then well and good. But if it is sincerely desirous of assisting in the cause of temperance, then I say that this Bill should provide for the appointment, under the direction of the Minister of Justice, of such officers as may be deemed necessary, in the different manufacturing and wholesale centres, for the purpose of seeing that this law is carried out.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I think it will be generally agreed that this legislation is the result of a general demand from the whole Dominion of Canada for a Dominion prohibitory law, and my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, in the different debates that have taken place, has sought to convince this House and to convince this country, that under this Bill he is giving the temperance people of Canada a much better, much more satisfactory, and a much more complete Bill for the suppression of the liquor traffic than would be a Dominion total prohibition law.
My hon. friend surely has seen from the discussion that has taken place since the Bill was introduced that in its present shape it is going to be absolutely a dead letter. I think I am not going too far when I say that it is going to be absolutely a dead letter by the wish and intention of the present Government. I do not think that they have any intention that it should be a help to prohibition. So far, they have refused to agree to the appointment of a prosecuting officer to look after infringements of the law. We have in the province of Saskatchewan prohibited the sale of liquor as a beverage. In the past, the great bulk of the liquor used in Saskatchewan has been purchased, as it is still, in Ontario or Quebec, chiefly in the city of Montreal. If an infringement of the Saskatchewan liquor law occurs in Toronto or in Montreal how can the temperance people of the province of Saskatchewan be expected to successfully prosecute the offenders. It would be an impossibility. The temperance people cannot take that duty on their hands. The Government of the province of Saskatchewan will look after the prosecution of offences that take place within that province, but who is going to look after the prosecution and punishment of offenders against the law of Saskatchewan in other provinces as provided in this Bill of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice. Unless a public prosecutor is appointed and paid for out of the Dominion funds, my hon. friend might just as well withdraw the Bill. It would be more satisfactory to the temperance people of Canada if that were done than to have it put on the statute book in the form proposed, with nobody to look after the prosecutions, and to have it become a dead letter, because the result of a law which becomes a dead letter is to bring the law into disrepute, and in this case it would be a blow to the temperance

people and to temperance sentiment throughout the country.
To my mind, there are only two ways of dealing with this question. The people of Canada, from one end of the Dominion to the other, have demanded a Dominion prohibitory law. If the Government cannot see its way clear to go so far, well and good; _but if they cannot, and they propose an Act which my hon. friend the Minister of Justice says will be of great .advantage to the temperance people, surely it is up to the Government to provide the necessary machinery for the carrying out of that law, in order that something may be accomplished along the lines desired by the temperance people. The officers of the province of Saskatchewan cannot come here and enforce this law. This will be a Dominion Act. Who can enforce it? Only the Dominion Government, and if it refuses to provide the necessary machinery for the enforcement of the law, the Act will certainly become a dead letter, and, as I have already said, not only of no use to the temperance people but a disadvantage and a detriment which will place them in a worse position than they are in now.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
It is quite evident
that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) has riot read this Bill. Its purpose is to aid provincial legislation by restricting the sale or use of intoxicating liquors. It is to be placed on the statute book for that purpose and any person who carries liquor into a province from any other province, or imports it into any province from any place outside of Canada is liable to a penalty.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: That is for the sale.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: That is, any person who imports into a province any liquor to be used in violation of the provisions of the provincial law. There is nothing in this Bill to prevent any person taking liquor into the province. There is nothing in the provincial legislation of Ontario which prevents a man from taking in liquor for his own use. There is nothing in the legislation of Manitoba which prevents it. Suppose that a man sends liquor from Montreal to Prince Edward Island; the person who carries that liquor into Prince Edward Island-

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
What about the man who sends it?
170J

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I will come to that. The man who delivers that liquor in Charlottetown is liable, and under our provincial law the liquor is liable to be seized. Suppose that the case which my hon. friend just put to me happened. The Provincial Government is liable for the administration of the law, and it can prosecute the man in Montreal who sends the liquor. Suppose that a man in the city of New Glasgow steals money from my hon. friend, and he goes to the city of Montreal and is arrested under a warrant issued in the town of New Glasgow; at whose expense would that be done? It would be at the expense of the Government of Nova Scotia. This Bill is to aid provincial legislation, and it will be effective if the law is enforced by the provinces. A change has come over the spirit of the dreams of hon. gentlemen opposite since this Bill was introduced. They were perfectly satisfied with it when it was introduced; they thought it was proper that it should be administered by the Provincial Governments. Now they want the Dominion Government to take charge of it, to pay for the enforcement of it, and to have it taken out of the hands of the Provincial Legislatures altogether.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I desire to entirely repudiate the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. McLean) that those of us who said we would favour the passing of a law by the Dominion Parliament to aid provincial legislation are bound to accept all the provisions of the Bill as introduced by the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice himself invited us to make suggestions which might improve the Bill, and, I am bound to say, with a very broad spirit he has accepted suggestions that have been made. That is what we are here for, at all events that is what hon gentlemen on this side of the House believe, and I am sorry to see my hon. friend from Queens take the view that it is his duty, not to suggest, but to support ail that the Government introduces and to cry " hear, hear."

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I did not say anything of the kind.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: During the whole discussion the hon. member for Queens has not made a single suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: He made one which I accepted.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: He must have seen the weaknesses in this Bill, and he ought to have suggested some improvement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: He suggested one.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Which one?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: He suggested that it be made clear that the clerk or agent, as well as the principal, would be liable, and I' adopted that suggestion at the same time as I adopted the amendment with regard to the railways.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I beg my hon. friend's pardon; I thought it was my hon. friend from Kings who made that suggestion. Then the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLean) set us a good example.
But the hon. gentleman does not draw the distinction between the offence which will be committed in a province where the liquor is received and the offence that may be committed in a distant province in sending the liquor either by steamer or railway. Of course, it is only when the liquor reaches its destination in prohibited territory that the offence is consummated, and this Bill provides, evidently and as the Minister of Justice thought it well that it should so provide, that prosecutions might take place at the point where the offence originates. What we complain of is that people living in distant parts of Canada, some in Prince Edward Island, some in the Northwest Territories, some away off 2,000 miles in Saskatchewan, into which territory liquor may go from week to week, or month to month, from the wholesale dealers and manufacturers in Ontario and Quebec, knowing how injurious it is that these things should be done, should he obliged-and the burden would rest largely upon the temperance people-to put their hands into their pockets if they are going to prosecute under this law, come down to Montreal or Toronto, spend a lot of time, waste a lot of money, and employ counsel at their own expense for the purpose of carrying on prosecutions at these centres. That is what we complain of and all we are asking the Government to do is to show that it appreciates, even in a small degree, the desirability from the standpoint of the people of Canada, of having this law enforced.
I would like to hear what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) has to say about this Bill. I would like to know whether he is one of those who are simply content to put a law on the statute book and then be able to say: all you have

to do is to look at the statutes and you will see that the Dominion Parliament has passed a law to assist in enforcing provincial prohibition. Is the Minister of Trade and Commerce content with that? He was for years and years, long before these other hon. gentlemen talked, or ever had a thought, about temperance, prominently known as a leading temperance advocate in this country, and as one who was in favour of the total abolition of the use. of intoxicating liquors. My hon. friend now comes from a province where in almost every county they had a prohibitory law many years ago under the Canada Temperance Act. He knows with what enthusiasm and with what eloquence he advocated the adoption of that law. My hon. friend must have watched its operation, he must have known how earnest the temperance people of the province were about the enforcement of that law, that they spent thousands upon thousands of dollars in seeking to enforce it, and how at last they became discouraged. He must know further that in most of the counties of New Brunswick the Canada Temperance Act is to-day a dead letter;
but, they have a law on the
5 p.m. statute book, as the Minister of Justice will have a law upon the statute book, if this Bill goes through. The Minister of Trade and Commerce knows just as well as he knows that he is reading a newspaper at this moment, that unless you appoint a public prosecutor to enforce a law of this kind the law will never be enforced. You will have a spasmodic enforcement for a little while but the people will then become discouraged and the law will become a dead letter. I agree entirely with what my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) has said that unless this Government makes provision for the enforcement, not of the provincial laws-we do not ask that-but of this law that it is asking * Parliament to put on the statute book, it cannot expect the people to believe that it is in earnest; that it sincerely desires that this law shall be a success and that by this means the cause of temperance will be promoted. May I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to give me the benefit of his view in regard to the absence of any provision in this Bill for the appointment of a prosecutor whose duty it will be to see that the law is enforced?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
This Bill seems to me to be a splendid measure and for this

reason: Let ns suppose that the enforcement of the law were in the hands of the Dominion Government; we will say that the Dominion has a Conservative Government and that there is in the province a Liberal Government. Knowing how deeply polities and partisanship have eaten into the life and being of this country, does anybody suppose for one minute that the cause of temperance would deter the Liberal Government of the province from making an exhibition of the administration of that law by the Dominion in that province, and making it so utterly and absolutely impossible and intolerable to the people that at the next federal election every man would vote against the Federal Government? That to my mind is one of the very strongest objections to the scheme proposed by the hon. member for St. John ('Mr. Pugsley). You have in addition to that, preserved in this legislation the sacred right of provincial autonomy. Now then, if a man is offended against outside of his own bailiwick, he is, as I understand it, and as I understand the principle of all law, required to put the law in motion himself at any distance or at any local point at which that local law is administered. If. the people of Ontario want prohibition they have it now within their grasp. Their objection has been heretofore that constitutionally they could not enact a full prohibitory law, and also that the Federal Government would not assist them because there would be an invasion of their territory by all sorts of liquor selling by freebooters who would bombard, as it were, the province in such a way that it would make their provincial law ineffective. The Dominion Government now says: we will stand aside, we will remove that objection, we will allow you to have full sway, we will put you in the position, that the entire Dominion will assist you in defending yourself and in making your Act effective. In order that this legislation may have its full value, we have only to look at the other side of the question. A province which does not wish to have a prohibitory law is not included in any vain attempt to carry out an impossibility. You have to preserve the distinct individualities of the provinces. If the province of Ontario wishes prohibition it need not sidestep it the way it is doing now but it can, according to the constitution, enact it and then pursue to the uttermost parts of this Dominion all offenders against the Act. This Bill removes all the objections in that respect and surely, for the reasons which I have given, and for other reasons too numerous to mention, it is far better that we should respect the rights of the provinces than that we should invade them and bring about a collision with the provinces with the hostility, the animosity and the possible disruption of this Dominion, that would result.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I am surprised that
my hon. friend takes such a serious view of this matter. When the question is the prosecution of a wholesale dealer in the city of Montreal or Toronto, no controversy between the local and Federal Government could possibly arise. The information is laid by some person who knows that the offence has been committed; it is a purely private matter; it is no part of the provincial Government's business to advise the Department of Justice what to do in the prosecution of any criminal. My hon. friend's statement is so wide Of the mark that I feel sure he cannot have read the Bill. He must not run away with the idea that this is a prohibitory measure. It is nothing of the kind. After this law comes in force, there will still be dozens of stills in the province of Ontario manufacturing liquor at different places, and dozens of bonded warehouses dotted all over the province offering this liquor for sale. The only thing this Bill prohibits is the sending of liquor into a prohibition province from outside, and we are simply making the reasonable request that this Government shall enforce this law ip outside provinces, and leave the province of Ontario, or any other prohibition province, to enforce its own law. I was a little disappointed at the attitude of my hon. friend from Queens (Mr. McLean) when he cited the case of Prince Edward Island. Let us suppose that an illicit dealer in Prince Edward Island orders a quantity of intoxicating liquor from a wholesale merchant in Montreal. The merchant ships it by the Intercolonial. It is addressed to the illicit dealer in Prince Edward Island; it is put on the train at Bonaventure Station, and is taken by the Intercolonial to Charlotte-where the illicit dealer takes possession of it. Now, all those concerned with the shipment are guilty. The first guilty party is the wholesale merchant in Montreal who sold the liquor to the illicit dealer in Prince Edward Island; then the Intercolonial is guilty for having carried the liquor into Prince Edward Island, and that is the only way in which liquor

can be carried into Prince Edward Island at certain seasons of the year. My hon. friend has heard the minister say that he will not prosecute the Intercolonial for carrying the liquor into Prince Edward Island, and therefore that criminal cannot be dealt with. If my hon. friend wished to prosecute the wholesale merchant in Montreal, he would have to prosecute him before some court in Montreal. I am surprised that the hon. member from Queens should advocate a system which would throw a duty of that kind upon his own province. Why does he not come in with us and ask the minister to . provide that when an offence of that kind is committed by a wholesale merchant in Montreal, Toronto, or any other large centre, the Dominion Government will undertake the duty of prosecuting the offender, just as it prosecutes offenders against the Inland Revenue Act, the Weights and Measures Act, the Fisheries Act, .and all similar Acts dealing with offences that may be committed in any part of the Dominion. That is what I should have expected my hon. friend to do.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: From the discussion that has taken place it is evident that this Bill is not quite as effective as the Government could make it. There were, no doubt, reasons that commended themselves to the Government why they should not introduce what is called Dominion-wide prohibition; but having decided to introduce a measure of this kind, I cannot understand why they hesitate to make it as effective as possible. I think the Bill would he strengthened by providing, as the hon. member for St. John has suggested, that prosecutions for offences committed outside of a prohibition province shall be taken care of by the Dominion Government. Of course, if that provision would not make the Bill any more effective, that is a good reason why the Government should decide against including it in the Bill. But if it would make it more effective, why does the minister refuse to insert it in the Bill? Why not make the Bill as effective as possible? No reason that has commended itself to the judgment of the committee has yet, I think, been given by the minister why the suggestion of my hon. friend should not be adopted. The suggestion certainly appeals to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.

I have not heard any good reason given yet why we should subvert the whole system of the administration of law in this country for the sake of this particular law. The hon. gentleman says 
my reasons are not good, but before discussing that, let me point out the utter inaccuracy of the hon. member for Guys-borough, who insists on saying that we have not provided any means by which there shall be a prosecution when goods are carried on the Intercolonial; if he has followed the discussion he must have observed that I openly accepted the suggestion of the hon. member for St. John, and it is in the Bill now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
This law will be enforced just as every other law of the same nature is enforced. It has been pointed out that we prosecute under the Inland Revenue Act. We collect the revenues of the Dominion, and we prosecute those who steal from the nation just as any man initiates proceedings when his property has

been stolen; but laws of this nature are left to be enforced primarily by people who may be injured by the action complained of, or, in the last resort, by the provincial authorities, and this law will be absolutely in the same situation. The hon. gentleman from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hughes) says: Oh, it would be more effective if we provided a special prosecutor. That would be quite true of all criminal laws; but, if we start to do that, we cannot differentiate, and as' was suggested by an hon. member who spoke a little while ago, we would have to establish a police and detective force in all parts of the Dominion to devote itself to hunting out violations of this liquor law. Why should that be suggested when there is throughout this country the officers of the provinces, all of them interested in enforcing the provincial laws? And this is a law to aid in the enforcement of the provincial laws. It is true that the offence of the man "who sends" is committed in one province, and in that respect it violates the law of the Dominion of Canada. It produces its ultimate result in another province, and there it violates the law of the Dominion, and by means of that liquor being sent in, there is brought about a violation of the law of that province. -It is suggested that the people interested in temperance in this country are so absolutely selfish and local that they do not care one straw about the violations of laws of this kind, enacted to enforce temperance laws, provided that you are not hitting them in their own province. Much has been said about Montreal and Toronto and the other great centres; that there will be nobody there to prosecute, and that a man will have to come all the way from the wilds of Saskatchewan to the wicked 'city of Montreal in order to lay his information and do his prosecuting. I can assure the hon. gentleman from St. John and all the other gentlemen anxious about the enforcement of this law that I know good earnest people in Montreal who will see that the wholesaler must not violate the law, and that the vendor of liquor who is violating the law, even though he is sending it to Saskatchewan, will have an information laid against him, and that the prosecution will go on like a prosecution under any other law.
It has been said: if we were honest in our desire, and if we were sincere, we would do this, that, or the other thing Suggestions of lack of sincerity or honesty are very easily made; but it is perhaps possible to
doubt the sincerity of suggestions that would attach to this measure the creation of an immensely expensive and I submit unnecessary machinery for its enforcement.
I have sufficient confidence in the people who are behind the temperance laws-and many of them, and the strongest and most sincere of them, have urged and commended this legislation-that, when we have given them the instrument for which they ask, they will not hesitate to use it, and I am satisfied that the apprehensions of my hon. friend from St. John will not be justified. I sincerely trust that I have given to the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Hughes) a reason that he at all events will accept as having some weight. I am particularly desirous of doing so, because I am glad to recognize that the hon. member for Kings does not find it necessary to make suggestions of lack of sincerity or honesty in regard to a proposal of this nature in order to back up his opinions. I accept his questioning as being intended to bring out the facts, and I really do think the fact has been brought out that we need not have any anxiety about the enforcing of this measure.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The minister said that the enforcement of this law would entail heavy expenditure, and that it would be unfair to place that upon the Dominion, but he also inferred that it would be quite right to put it upon the shoulders of private individuals, such as the temperance people.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
In the first place, the provinces already have machinery in connection with the enforcement of their own laws, so that they would not have to create new machinery. So far as the operation of the temperance people are concerned, they may be carried on whether we have a prosecutor or not, and the work in any one particular city or toym does not entail very heavy expense; but if we had to provide a special force scattered throughout the Dominion, away up into the wilds of Saskatchewan as well as in the wicked cities of Montreal and Toronto, and in other places, that would impose a tremendous burden upon this Dominion of Canada. More than that, it is asking us to set a precedent. If we are going to provide that special macliinery for the enforcement of this law, I confess that I do not see what reason there is why we should not provide a similar machinery for the

enforcement of laws the offences against which, however grave one might regard the offences against this law, are certainly much graver than those contemplated by this law. I have heard it put forward that this Government should not provide laws that were desirable because this Government was not going to proceed to enforce them. The sentiment that is behind this law can be trusted to see to its enforcement.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.

speechtext: Carried.

speechtext: We do not do that at all. We speak of them as being cities where to-day it happens that there are large manufactories of intoxicating liquor. We do not suggest for a single moment that they are not just as moral cities as any other cities in Canada.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I have nothing to apologize for. The Minister of Justice asked why we should treat this law in a different manner from the other laws which are placed upon the statute book, the enforcement of which is left to the provincial authorities. The reason is that a vast majority of the people of this country think that the Dominion, as a whole, is deeply interested in the prevention of the use of intoxicating liquors. The people who have petitioned this Government for the passage of a Dominion prohibitory law have put forward very strongly the fact that by the use of intoxicating liquors there is a great waste of energy and money, and that particularly during the war, that waste should be prevented as far as possible, and the resources and energy and strength of the people

should be conserved for the purposes of state, which means for the purposes of Canada. I can see, but my hon. friend the minister cannot see the very great difference between the duty of the Dominion Government so far as the enforcement of this law is concerned from what it is in regard to the enforcement of hundreds of criminal statutes which are law in the country. The very nature of the business which is sought to be prevented also makes it desirable to treat it from an entirely different standpoint. That is a view I have endeavoured to present, and I can see the very strongest reason why this Government should do what it reasonably can by the appointment of officers to secure the enforcement of the law.

subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to give us some example of laws which are enforced by the Dominion now-precisely similar laws-

subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Fisheries.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Never mind, thank
you-precisely similar laws which are enforced in the way he suggests this should be' enforced.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Take the fisheries laws as suggested by my hon. friend from Guys-borough. We know that there are laws relating to the rivers of Canada, both tidal and non-tidal, prohibiting fishing on Sunday, prohibiting fishing in certain seasons of the year, prohibiting the obstruction of tidal waters by nets. The Dominion does not own the fish, but regards it as being to the advantage of the people of this Country that the fisheries should be conserved and protected, and the production of fish increased as much as possible. The fishery laws are enforced absolutely at the expense of the Dominion treasury. The Dominion has its fishery guardians to see to the enforcement of the law, and when offenders are arrested the Dominion confiscates the nets or rods, the Dominion employs counsel, prosecutes, and bears the expense of the enforcement of the law.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Is that a purely provincial matter?
