speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Then I am not asking about that. Hive us one case of a law of this kind.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
This is a Dominion matter, just as the enforcement of the fishing

laws is a Dominion matter. Surely, this pertains to the interest and welfare of the whole Dominion.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
That is begging the
question.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon.
friend is seeking to find a reason for defending this Government by defending the measure now' before the committee. I am obliged to assume he is very sincere, but I am afraid he is very prejudiced, which is, perhaps, not an unusual condition for my hon. friend to be in, and perhaps he is hardly to blame for it. I think it is of Dominion-wide importance that this law should be enforced. I agree with hon. members on this side who have spoken that, unless you have a criminal law properly enforced you not only create a contempt on the part of the people for that particular law, but you tend to create contempt for all criminal laws. In this matter, Parliament surely ought to be guided by the experience of the past. I am glad that the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) has come into the Chamber. He knows perfectly well that where the prohibitory laws in the province in which he was born-and which had the honour of having him for a good many years as one of its representatives in this Parliament-have not been enforced, it has been because there were no proper officials to enforce them. He knows that the burdens of such enforcement are too heavy to be borne by private individuals or by the temperance organizations of the province. The Minister of Justice-I trust he will pardon me for repeating my observations; I cannot help repeating them because he still seems to pursue the wrong course and to be guided by wrong views as to the importance of these laws-must clearly understand that, so far as the enforcement of provincial laws is concerned, we do not ask this Government to appoint public prosecutors. We say that the most effective way in which you can assist provincial legislation is to allow prosecutions to take place	in those	very centres
where the offence originates, where the liquor is manufactured, and from which it has been shipped. If he knows anything of what has been done in the past in reference to shipments of liquor to Prince Edward Island and other places where prohibition is in force, he knows that liquor is sent under various disguises,-sent, sometimes as groceries, sometimes as pickles, and
so on. These gentlemen in Montreal-not these wicked gentlemen, but these astute gentlemen-engaged in the manufacture of liquor, know a thing or two about the way to deceive the transportation companies and the authbrities, and they send the liquor into prohibited sections of Canada as the most innocent articles of merchandise you can imagine. The Minister of Justice himself admits that it is desirable to have some provision for prosecuting these manufacturers and distillers who may seek to send liquor into prohibited territory. That being the case, does it not raise the question of proceedings being taken outside the province immediately affected, perhaps hundreds of miles away from that province. It is that extra-provincial prosecution, it is that Dominion prosecution, which we want this Government to undertake. We want simply that the phase of the law which provides that a manufacturer or wholesaler who sends liquor into prohibited territory may be proceeded against shall be enforced by officers provided by the Dominion Government. That is all that we ask; and we say to you, Mr. Minister, with all sincerity that, unless you do appoint public prosecutors at the expense of this Dominion, whose duty it shall be to ferret out violations of the law, and to punish offenders, you may just as well stop the passage of this Bill, for you will be simply putting upon the statute book a measure which, while you say it will aid provincial legislation, will really be a mere pretense, a merely farcical piece of legislation, absolutely nugatory, and which you yourself some day, will be ashamed of and will wish you had never placed upon the statute book.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman give us a concrete case of such a prosecution-just take one.
Mr. PUGSLEY- I will give a concrete instance of what such a prosecution would be, if that is what the hon. gentleman means?	.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: All right.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Suppose a manufacturer or wholesaler sends liquor into a province in which prohibition is in force, the liquor being intended for sale in that province, that manufacturer or wholesaler is liable under this Bill. The offence, let us say, originates in some city in Ontario or Quebec, but is consummated in Prince Edward Island. We say that this is a case that ought to be attended to and carried to. a

conclusion by the Dominion Government. So far as offences within the province are concerned, we are quite willing that the provincial authorities should bear the responsibility. But, when the burden has to be borne of going into another province, perhaps many hundreds of miles distant, the prosecution can be better attended to by officials of the Dominion Government than by the provincial authority, and therefore we say it shpuld be looked after by the Dominion. We also wish to urge and this is the last word I shall have to say^in regard to this matter

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Gentlemen on the other side treat this Bill as if it were a joke, something of the least possible importance merely to be carried through and placed upon the statute book, that they may boast of what they have done, being quite satisfied to leave the law merely nugatory. All I nave to say about this feature of the Bill is, that if you pass the Bill in its present form, the legislation, will be simply on paper and will not be effective, and might better never have been enacted at all. We have said all we' can, and responsibility must rest upon hon. gentlemen on the Treasury Benches and their supporters behind them who are evidently not desirous of having a measure on the statute-book that there will be any hope of being made effective.
Amendment to amendment agreed to.

speechtext:
I have an amendment
to propose, if this is the right time. I move:
No license shall hereafter be granted or renewed, under the provisions of the Inland Revenue Act, to any person to enable such person to carry on business as a distiller, brewer or maltster in any province wherein a Provincial Act is in force prohibiting the sale of intoxicating liquor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
A suggestion on the lines of this amendment was made the other evening by the hon. member for South Wellington. I do not know that I need repeat at length what I then said. The proposal involves our making an absolute prohibition of manufacturing because the province has made a prohibition of pale, and so it is not on the lines on whicn this Bill proceeds. It is not in accordance with the principle of this measure, which principle was endorsed by a very large majority of this House, namely, that our legislation should be in the direction of making effective legislation adopted by the prov-

inces. It is suggested that because a province has prohibited one thing, we should legislate to prohibit another and a different thing, both of them being things within the province. For the reasons which I gave the other evening, and which will be luund upon Hansard, I feel that I cannot accept this suggested amendment.
Amendment negatived on division.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), when this Bill was last up, gave notice of another amendment in connection with this section. As it appears in the Votes and Proceedings, it is to be an amendment to section 3. I am quite satisfied the intention was to add the following as section 3 of the Bill:
Every one is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a penalty not exceeding tyro hundred dollars, or to imprisonment for six months, or to both fine and imprisonment, who: '
(a)	Sends or ships by any public conveyance to any place in which the sale of intoxicating liquor is prohibited, any package containing intoxicating liquor not plainly labelled so as to show the actual contents of such package; or
(b)	Sends or ships by any public conveyance any package containing intoxicating liquor addressed to a fictitious person, or addressed otherwise than to the actual consignee of such package; or
(c)	Being a common carrier or the servant or agent of a common carrier, knowingly receives for conveyance, carries or makes delivery of any such package; or
(d)	Knowingly takes delivery from any common carrier of any such package.
The purpose of the amendment is to thwart the endeavours of people who seek secretly to introduce liquor into a province in which there is a law prohibiting sale, the requirement being that all such packages should be plainly labelled, showing their contents. The different sections provide for the different offences that may be committed in connection with such packages.

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: The minister accepts the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: I am prepared to accept the amendment. It may very well be that we ought to modify the wording to meet a suggestion made in connection with the Intercolonial. There are provisions there with regard to carriers. I would move that we add in subsection i(e), after the words, "servant or agent of a common carrier," the words, "or of any Government railway, Dominion or provincial."

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: With regard to the employees of a Government railway, could the minister not put something in the Bill

that would guard the minor official? I think that the Intercolonial railway should be in exactly the same position as the ordinary railway company, but, of course, the ordinary railway company could be proceeded against. It seems to me that it would be hardly fair to proceed against a minor employee who was simply doing his duty on the Government railway. Take, for instance, the baggage master, or the brakeman, or the conductor, or the engineer; they should not be held liable. It seems to me that the parties held liable should be the officials- who receive and the officials who deliver the goods. I dp not know how the minister would work it out, but take, for instance, the agent at Shediac.
A package might come consigned to Prince Edward Island. Or take the carter who transfers the package from the cars to the steamer. He might suspect it to contain liquor, but he could not exercise his judgment. He has no right to refuse the package; it is his duty to send it on. But should he be held liable? I think the point is worthy of consideration.
Mr .DOHERTY: We are in this situation : We do mean to say to that man, and to strengthen his position by putting the law behind him, that whatever may be the instructions of his superiors, he is not to do that if he knows that the package contains liquor, and it is not properly labelled. The law does propose to step in between any superior officer on the Intercolonial railway and any inferior officer, and to say to them all equally: You shall not take or carry liquor unless it is properly labelled. . I hardly think we can assume that the superior officer will dismiss a man for obeying the law. If he does he puts himself in a position of ordering or authorizing that man to break the law, and it seems to me he would make himself responsible. But after we have made it perfectly clear that we mean this legislation to apply to [DOT] every person on the Intercolonial railway, does the hon. gentleman apprehend that the minister, or the general manager, would give instructions that the Intercolonial employees should violate the law?

What I want to do is to guard the inferior employee against wrongdoing. We know that the Crown is some times very merciless. I have known ou the Intercolonial cases where men doing their duty have violated the law, and damages were recovered against them, and the Government did not stand behind them
as an ordinary railway company would. Can it not be provided that, where the employee of the Government railway is simply acting in the discharge of his duty, and is carrying out his instructions, the general manager be held liable. Let the general manager take the place of the railway company and then, of course, in the event of damages being recovered from him, he would be recouped by the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are dealing with the criminal law and it seems to me that to make the general manager responsible for something with which he had nothing to do would be acting more harshly than if we were to say to the employee: You must not do this. Before an employee could be convicted, it would have to be shown that he had knowingly violated the law. I think it is important that the law should make it quite clear that nobody is to do this knowingly, and that it will not do to plead instructions from a superior officer. Once this law is passed and made applicable to all the people that come under it, the situation of the servant who, under the instructions of his master, knowingly violated this law, would be in the position of a servant whose master told him to steal a package of goods. It would not avail him to say that his superior had told him to violate the law. I felt the desirability of making this special provision with regard to the first section of the Bill so as to cover those employees for the reason that as the Bill does not apply to the Crown and the offence is an offence created by the proposed Act, there might have been a loophole of escape from what I believe to be the general law. I think the possibility of hardship is very remote. It is desirable, if you are going to have an effective law, that every man who has to do with the handling or carrying of goods should be brought under its operation. Any employee of any carrier dismissed for obeying the law, iat all events, if he had a contract of any kind with his employer, would certainly have grounds for an action for improper dismissal. When we know how eloquently dismissed officials are defended in *the House on occasion, if this case should arise, certainly any such grievance would not be unheard of.
If there are several persons, can they all be prosecuted ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, you may have many parties to the same offence.

Mr. CO'PP: Suppose a number of packages of liquor are shipped from Montreal, some of 'which are consigned to Quebec, where there may not be a prohibitory law, and some to New Brunswick where we hope, with the proposed legislation, we will have a prohibitory law; when the train gets to Campbellton, near the border line between Quebec and New Brunswick, the train is taken charge of by a new set of men, and when the train gets to Newcastle there will be found, amongst other goods sent from Montreal, a package of liquor consigned to somebody in Newcastle. The brakeman, whose duty it is to look after the train, throws off this package along with others. The liquor, or prohibition, inspector of the province is on hand; he sees the brakeman putting off that package and he at once takes his name and lays information against fum. Here is a perfectly, innocent man working upon the train who delivers this parcel along with others. The inspector, under the law, has a right to take this man's name and to at once take proceedings against him for breaking the law. I contend that the brakeman, or the Intercolonial employee, who is absolutely innocent, should not be mulcted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He will not be.
He may be. %

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The law only says that if he "knowingly" does it he will be liable.
But, if this package of liquor is on his train and he gets an order to put it off, it is his duty to unload it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then if he does he ceases to be doing his duty; he should leave it alone.
What will he do with it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Leave it there.
Where will he take it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If he is a wise man, the law saying that it must not be " taken," he will not take it anywhere.
But it is on the train, he is in charge of the train and what is he going to do with it-throw it off and destroy it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not know that brakemen were in charge of trains; but, whoever put that on the taain is responsible for having it there. If the brakeman lets it severely alone, as I would advise him to do; I cannot see what he is going to be convicted of.
But in all probability the minister will not be there to advise the brakeman and he will not know what his duty is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman will transmit the advice; he has the brakeman in his eye. I move that the committee rise and report progress.

Is that amendment
adopted ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No.
Progress reported.
