What is included under " mail service?"

Rural mail service, steamship mail service, and the ordinary service iby land. The Transcontinental railway, running through new territory in the province of Quebec, and the Canadian Northern, opening up territory in other parts of the country, account for an increase of $19,932. The balance of the increase, $385,000, is accounted for by rural mail delivery and the ordinary mail service.
How much of that increase is due to rural mail delivery?

The greater part of the $385,000 is on account of rural mail delivery. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) asked me to bring down a detailed statement of the increased expenditure on rural mail delivery since 1908. It is as follows: 1908-9, $6,212; 1909-10, $19,615; 1910-11, $60,022; 1912-13, $86,355; 1913-14, $290,700; 1914-15, $477,945, making a total of' $940,849.

If I remember correctly, an effort was made some years ago to change the method of granting mail subsidies, and it was proposed to pay a certain amount to any steamship line that carried our mail. Originally, the subsidies were more restricted than of recent years. What steamship lines are getting mail subsidies?

Properly speaking, the steamship subsidy does not come under my

department, but under the Department of Trade and Commerce. One of the conditions of the contract entered into between these subsidized steamship lines and the Government is that they shall carry the mail. Heretofore, subsidies have been granted to the Canadian Pacific Steamship Line, the Allan Line, the White Star, the Canadian Northern-in fact, all the principal lines sailing from the St. Lawrence. As my hon. friend knows, the Canadian Pacific and the Allan Line are now amalgamated and that is the only line running now.

Has the war interfered
very much with the mail service?
Very much.
A good deal of our mail goes via New York?
Most of it does, because steamships sailing from that port are generally faster than the lines on the Canadian route, and they give a more frequent service.
Could the minis-ier give us the aggregate cost of the conveyance of mail by land and by railways for the years 1913, 1914 and 1915?
I could get these figures for my hon. friend during the evening.
This afternoon the right hon. leader of the Opposition asked a question as to the censorship of mail coming from the United States to Canada. Does that apply both ways?
Yes.
And to private correspondence as well?

All. I would rather
my hon. friend did not pursue these inquiries.

As the fiscal year 1915-16 has been ended for some days, could *the minister give us a summary of the result of the operations of his department for the past twelve months? I would remind the minister that he promised us an estimate of the revenue derived from the war stamps, showing what properly belonged to the department and what to consolidated revenue.

As to the first question put by my hon. friend, I will remind him that I gave the figures some time ago in answer, I think, to my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). It is estimated
that the department will receive about $6,000,000 from the war stamp tax.

What were the figures
that the minister gave to the hon. member for Rouville the other night?

I cannot give them
offhand.
Does the minister remember roughly what the revenue and the expenditure were?
I do not. I think the figures were given in answer to my hon. friend himself; they were brought down to the end of December.

I got a statement down to the end of December.
Mr. iCAiSGRAIN : And for certain offices in the principal cities we brought the figures down to the end of February.
I want to find out the probable receipts of the department for the year ended March 31, 1916, and also the probable expenditures. .
I will give the information in a few minutes.

In the statement which
the minister has given for rural mail deliveries for 1914-15, viz.: $477,945, can he tell us how that is distributed amongst the different provinces?

Those figures I also
gave the other day; they are on Hansard.
There is an item for salaries and allowances. I presume that refers to salaries of postmasters.
Yes, not to all postmasters, because the great majority of the postmasters are paid by commission.
Does that item include what is allowed in commissions?
No, simply the salaries to those who are paid salaries.

What does " allowances "
mean?

There is a provisional
allowance given to all employees west of Sault Ste. Marie on account of the higher rate of living west of that point. It has been given for years.
That is an advantage which the western employees have over the eastern employees.
It is not an advantage, because it costs more to live west of Sault Ste. Marie than it does in the East.

Is there anything in the
Estimates or in the report of the Postmaster General to show what commissions are paid to the different postmasters in the rural districts?
Fifty per cent on receipts of $1,000 ; 30 per cent from $1,000 to $10,000 and 20 per cent over $10,000.

That is the information I have. After the prorogation of the House last year a constituent of mine asked me if the postmasters would be allowed the same commission on the sale of what was alleged to be the extra war stamp of one cent, which came into force last session, as on the sale of the ordinary stamps. Is that the case?

No. The department has come to the conclusion that, as there is now no more work entailed upon the postmasters than before the tax was imposed, the sales of those stamps will not be counted for purposes of commission.
' The postmasters will get their commissions on the ordinary revenue, not including the war tax.
When did that regulation come into force?

The commission cannot be computed until all the returns are in. Therefore, for the year ended March 31, 1916, the commission will be computed when we get all the returns in from the different postmasters up to that date, and the salaries will be fixed for the year.
The commission on the sales of the extra alleged war stamp will be deducted.
The postmasters will get no commission on the sales of war stamps.
That is an arrangement that is coming into force now? '
Yes.
It is to be retroactive.

It is not really to be retroactive. The only way in which we can compute what the commission will be is by waiting for the returns for the fiscal year which has just closed, and then fixing the commission. In fixing the commission we will not take into consideration the sales of the extra war stamp.
No commission will be allowed to postmasters for sales of war stamps?
That is right.

As rural mail delivery has been extending, post offices have been eliminated. Can the minister tell the House how many postmasters have been done away with throughout Canada as rural mail deliveries have been extended, and what amount has been saved in that manner?

I could give my hon. friend the information as to the nuhaber of postmasters who have ceased to be postmasters, but that would take some little time to compute. I do not think that the saving will be very great, because in many instances the cost of rural mail delivery will be more than the amount paid to the postmaster.
Can the minister give any approximate idea of how many postmasters have been eliminated?
No, I would not like to give any approximate figures. I would rather bring down the exact figures.
That will be all right.

I \ ould like to ask the minister one favour, and that is, to send a representative of his department to the county of Inverness to examine the way in which his department has juggled the post offices in the district of Southwest Margaree and Creignish. He has established five or six post offices within a radius of three miles, instead of two as before. Our difficulty there is that the people who are *supposed to be served by those post offices, who were formerly served by two offices, will have to go the round of five new offices before they can be satisfied that there is no mail for them. These post offices are Kiltarlity, Scottsville, Mount Borden, Gil-lisdale, and one other post office within a radius of four miles. And the funny part of the whole thing is, that the man in a part of the district formerly served by Upper Margaree post office, if he wants to get his letter or newspaper that has been addressed to him, may have to make the round of the five offices. The minister will see that I am pretty well conversant with the circumstances, otherwise it might be destructive to my political standing to find fault with the multiplying of offices there; *but the fact is I am not finding fault with increasing the number of post offices. I want to show that these offices were

opened for political purposes, and the only reason I know of for placing the offices where they are was to give an office to John Jones here, to Tom Smith there, and to others who were faithful friends of the party in power. If the offices were located properly, I should be quite willing-I know how these things are done; I am human- that the friends of the Postmaster General should get appointments when new offices are opened. But it' is ridiculous that five different offices should be opened up within a narrow radius in a thinly-settled county, when other portions of the same county are not efficiently served. On the line from Dunvegan to St. Rose there is not a post office for six or seven miles, though this is a fairly thickly settled country. But in other cases there are four post offices not more than a mile or a mile and a half apart. It was found necessary to dismiss certain postmasters, friends of mine and of the party I support, and to give these offices to other people, who, of course, had to be of the other political persuasion. I am going to ask the minister to be kind enough to send somebody to investigate, and if he does not tell me, when I see him next session, that I am correct I will not ask any more favours. While I am on my feet I wish to say a word on the subject of mail contracts. I was astounded to hear that the department of the Postmaster General respected the system of tender and contract. That is the most marvellous thing I have ever heard. The system of tender and contract is the last thing we hear of in my county. To show the ridiculousness of the procedure, as followed in my county, let me refer to the Mabou-Whycooomagh route contract, and to the Invemess-Margaree service. The department followed the ordinary course in looking for tenders. They put up notices, and so on, and a number of men tendered. As it happened, the lowest tenderer in each case was a Liberal. The department decided, from some information they got from the gentleman who was the patronage-vendor-I do not mean any disrespect by that, I refer to the man who represents the Government, and who, no doubt, informed the Post Office Department-that it would not be right to give these men the contracts. So, correspondence was carried on with the agent there until finally it was discovered that there was a man who would take the contract for a dollar or two, or perhaps fifty cents less than the .lowest tenderer. This is the case of the Mabou-Whycocomagh service, and the
same condition obtained with regard to the Inverness-Margaree service. The reason I specify these is that they are substantial contracts, where the mail is carried, in one case, over a route of eighteen to twenty miles, and, in the other, of about twenty-five miles. The men who have these contracts are not getting rich. If it were a case where the lowest tenderer was asking too much for the service the department would be justified in investigating. But this was a case in which none of the tenderers was anything too low. If the man who sent in the highest tender had got the contract, he would only have starvation wages. I bring forward this case in order to show the fact that the object was to eliminate the Liberals. But what has been the result? No respectable Liberal would waste his time putting his name to the tender for a contract. In the first place, he knows his trouble would be wasted, for he could not get the contract, and, in the second place, he does not want to place himself in opposition to his neighbour who wants to get the contract at a paying price, so he says to himself he cannot hope to get the contract even if he were the lowest tenderer, and therefore he will leave it to the Tories. I do not often take up the time of the House; it is only when I have great reason that I speak here at all. In this case I have great reason. The reason is, to show the Postmaster General that he is destroying the essential feature of the system of tender and contract. If the papers destroyed in the great fire on Parliament Hill could be restored, I could read to the minister the names of twenty contracts, in every one of which a Liberal happened to be the lowest tenderer, and yet did not get the contract, because the patronage vendor corresponded with the department, and, by dint of time and correspondence, they succeeded in getting some Tory to take the contract at a few cents lower.	Even
in the small contracts, such a contract as that for the carrying of the mail from the station at Inverness to the post office, a distance of five or six hundred yards-even that could not be given to the lowest tenderer, but had to be given to some friend of the party in power. I must tell the Postmaster General that when my friends were in power they did not hand out to me the treatment he is handing out to his friends. When I asked to play the game that he is playing to-day-this is

open confession; I do not pretend to be holier than the rest-I was shown the door, in a very polite way, and I had to leave. The ridiculousness of such a thing was pointed out to me, and I had common sense enough to see it, and did not carry the agitation further. In every case, during the years I had to do with patronage, the contract went to the lowest tenderer, and in seventy-five per cent of the cases they went to Tories.
Mr. -CASGRAIN:	When were these five
post offices established, to which the hon. gentleman refers?

It was since 1911.
These post offices spring up at the most uncertain times, but particularly if there is a municipal election or a provincial local election pending. It is consequently impossible for me to remember When new offices are opened in/ a large county such as I represent. Perhaps I discover the creation of a new post office by being told, when I go to mail a letter to a patient in some district, that he may not get it for weeks, as new post offices have been opened in his neighbourhood. Of these five post offices to which I have referred, one was opened last year and one the year before.
Post Office Department-miscellarieous, $843,838.
Has the minister the information about these tenders?

I have heard of a great many contracts where the lowest tenders were not accepted because somebody else tendered below the figure mentioned, but I have not heard anybody say the contracts were let out at too high a figure.
We are not talking about that.

I know, but there must be some public interest at stake. Surely the complaint is not simply that good Liberals like those my hon. friend spoke of did not get the contracts. There must be something higher than that; the public interest must come in.

Do you think it is in the public interest to go behind tenders and award contracts privately at a figure a little below the lowest tenderer? Will the minister say that is in the public interest, or in the interest of decent administration of a public department?

I was surprised to hear my hon. friend say that he knows of 20 cases in which that was done. That is not the practice of the department. The practice is that the lowest tender is accepted, and, so far as I know, no consideration is given to the question whether a man is a Conservative or a Liberal. That is the way I administer the department, and the way I intend to administer it.

I am convinced of the truth of what I say and I tell the minister here, that no public consideration was brought into the decision that was arrived at respecting these two contracts and several others, because I know the parties who tendered and what they tendered for. I know that the men who tendered and expected to get the contracts came to me and told me they were surprised that they were not getting them. I told them I had a suspicion that someone else was after them. I know this is the system that was carried out with respect to these contracts anyway, and that no public interest was served by taking the contracts from the lowest tenderer and handing them over to party friends because they happened to be 75 cents or $2 or $3 lower.

I think this matter is of sumcient importance to justify the committee in securing from the minister, if possible, some declaration of departmental policy in repect of the system of tender and contract. I cited a case to the House the other day in reference to which information was furnished in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll). In that case it appeared that one Donald McIntosh had tendered at $350, and Joseph Duffy at $400, for a certain mail contract in the county of Cape Breton. It appears, according to the answer furnished, that Mr. Duffy was allowed to reduce his tender to $345, just $5 under the amount of the lowest tender. Three other cases similar to this were mentioned in reference to which answers supplied by the department during the present session disclosed the same state of facts. The hon. member for Inverness has referred to two cases of a similar nature, and I am quite satisfied from what I hear in Nova Scotia that there are scores and hundreds of cases where the system of tender and contract is not respected. But the minister enunciates a very different principle, and I am seriously disappointed to hear him take that position, namely that he is justified in awarding

a contract to some person who is permitted to make secretly an offer a little below the lowest tender. The minister says that if he gets a figure below the lowest tender, he is	justified in accepting it;
that the public interest has not suffered,	and therefore his action
is not open to criticism. The administration of the Post Office Department is a very important portion of the public service of this country, and if the minister goes behind the system of tender and contract and makes it a practice of the department to receive offers secretly from persons not tendering, accepting these offers just because they are below the amount of the lowest tender, all of which is done in violation of statute, I say that the administration of the department is open to the most serious criticism imaginable, and I cannot understand anything that could be done by any administrator or any minister of the Crown that would be more censura/ble, more disreputable, and more against the public interest. I do not know how far the present Postmaster General is responsible for that. I said the other day that the administration of his department was debauched by his predecessor in office. I repeat it now.
Tell us in what way?
It would take too long.
It will not take long.
Oh, it is admitted.

My hon. friend knows
that he and his colleagues felt the truth of my statement so much that they were very glad to get rid of their late colleague.
That is absolutely incorrect.
That is the view of the present Minister of Public Works, but I think my statement is absolutely correct.
Absolutely incorrect.

Whether it is the case or not, I say it is a good thing for the country that the late minister happened to get out anyway, owing to the character of his administration of the department. The present Postmaster General does not indicate any desire in practice, although he does in profession upon the floor of the House, to reform that department. If he would frankly admit that in the cases cited to him in reference to the violation of the sacredness of the system of tender and contract, this was done without his knowledge and that he

officially disapproved of it, and would give the committee and the House his promise that it would not occur in the future, perhaps we should be obliged to accept his statement. But he defends the practice of violating the system of tender and contract. I say that is as much a crime against the public service as is open theft, and he has no right, and his department has no right, to violate that system except under very extraordinary circumstances. It may be that this practice is more common in my own province than anywhere else. If so I am very sorry for that, and it may be due to the fact that the Government have not the right sort of political advisers in my province. If that is the case, the minister should take some warning from the facts which have been given him in this connection and refuse to have further correspondence with prospective Conservative candidates in Nova Scotia-and perhaps it would be well for him to administer some rebuke to those who are now Conservative members from that province. 'I want to hear some statement from the minister as to what will be the practice of the department in the future, and I think he should make an open confession here-whether he shall get absolution or not is another matter-that the practice of disregarding the system of tender and eontract is against his judgment and against the public interest.

(Translation): Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in the discussion on the means taken by the Postmaster General to cut down as much as possible the price of contracts.
I listened quite attentively to my hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean) when he stated that the officers of the Post Office Department may be carrying on a kind of haggling in the awarding of contracts. I would remind my hon. friend that the present Postmaster General is not the first one to be guilty of that crime, and I myself know of many precedents. In my own constituency, the inspector of the Quebec division went from one parish to another stating that the tenders were too high, .and succeeded in getting a reduction of five or ten dollars on the price of contracts. Such a course was in the public interest and was taken because the tenders received at the department were excessive.
If, however, the same practice obtained which is criticised to-day, because it was thought to be in the public interest and because the Post Office Department had to

meet a huge expenditure, so that it became necessary to control those expenses, it seems to me that the present minister is not to be blamed for doing what was done by his predecessors.
As I understand it, he has extended enormously the rural mail service, which has required a vast increase in the expenditure. So, taking advantage of similar circumstances, and on account of the great expenses incurred, I think he should be allowed, as were his predecessors, to take means to reduce in every way possible the figures of mail contracts.
Personally, I do not believe that the present minister blundered any more than his predecessors, especially, as may be gathered from the public accounts, when an account is taken of the fact that the Canadian people and the Canadian farmer now have an improved mail service, the best yet established, without any undue increase in the expenditure.

If there is one hon. gentleman more qualified tHan another to speak of the practices of both parties, it is my hon. friend (Mr. Girard), who has just sat down. I am not going to pursue his argument that the same methods as those now practised were carried on under the previous administration, more than to point out that between the case of a renewal of a contract, where, perhaps, the old contractor was allowed to reduce his tender $5 so that he might, without interruption to the service, continue the work, and the case of where tenders called for an altogether new system and a new route in which the highest tenderer was allowed to reduce his figures, there is a great difference in principle. I will tell the Postmaster General of a case which happened in the. county of Huntingdon-I do not think it was under his administration; I think it was under that of his immediate predecessor-where some post offices were closed. The rural mail system was being introduced and the lowest tenderer was a man who for thirty years had been the postmaster at the point of departure for the rural mail delivery. He was a one-armed man, and had been given the postmastership to enable him to make his livelihood. He had acted as postmaster for twenty-five or thirty years to the satisfaction of the whole community. When tenders were asked for the rural mail delivery it was hoped that this man, who, it was known, would be out of business as postmaster, as the rural mail system was to be introduced, would get the contract.

The fact that he was the lowest tenderer did 'not satisfy the local political heelers, and they so manipulated matters that another half mile was tacked on to the route, and the contract was given to another man. The place, I may say, was Dundee. I have not a word to say against the man who got the contract; I think he is doing the work fairly well, but I submit that it was scarcely fair that the man who had served as postmaster for twenty-five years, and who was the lowest tenderer, should be set aside and not given a chance. My hon. friends from Nova Scotia are, therefore, not quite .right when they hint that there are practices in Nova Scotia that are not carried on in the other provinces. This is one instance in the county of Huntingdon where the same methods of manipulation have been practised.

It is indeed amusing, if nothing else, to listen to hon. gentlemen opposite venturing to discuss political partisanship in connection with the administration of the Poet Office Department in various parts of Canada. I would not have interrupted, had it not been for the statement made by my hon. friend, the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) in which he cast a reflection upon my late colleague, the Hon. Mr. Pelletier, now Mr. Justice Pelletier. Let me say that few men, if any, have, ever undertaken to administer any department of the Government in this country who had greater difficulties to contend with than the late Postmaster General, by reason of the fact that, when Mr. Pelletier took charge of the Post Office Department, he had to deal with an organized Liberal party within the bounds of the department through the appointment in various parts of Canada, of active Liberal workers, not postmasters alone, but officials in other important branches of the department over which he presided.
Suppose my hon. friend gives us a little evidence in support of that statement.

My hon. friend is anxious to have evidence. I too was anxious to have evidence in support of the statement he made that the late Postmaster General was guilty of debauching-I think that was the term he used-the Post Office Department of this country. My hon. friend is anxious to have evidence, and I am always ready to accommodate my hon. friend, or any other hon. gentleman on the other

side of the House, and I -will at once meet his wish in that connection. I hold in my hand a letter headed:
Central Information Office of the Canadian Liberal Party.
Telephone No. Queen 8700.
Rooms 606-612, Hope Chambers, 63 Sparks street.
What is the height of the building? ,

This central information office is under the authority of the right hon. the leader of the Opposition. The letter reads:
My dear sir,-The first pamphlets issued by this office have been distributed and copies have been mailed you, and also to every Liberal worker in Canada whose name and address has been sent to this office. As you are aware we have not yet received the list of active workers, about which we have previously written you, and, consequently we are unable to extend our distribution into your territory. This means that none of the leading Liberals in your locality are benefiting by the information sent out from this office. Would you not make an extra effort and let us have your list of active workers at once.
Several other bulletins are now in the hands of the printer and are expected daily. These we also want to distribute.
Pray let us hear from you by return mail. We are now distributing these pamphlets in over 10,000 polls in Canada. Let us add your territory to this number.
Tours faithfully,
C. M. Goddard, Secretary.

What is .the date
of that fetter?

January 18, 1913, and
it is addressed to the postmaster of Poplar Point, Manitoba. It is amusing to hear from my hon. friend talk of political partisanship. When the late Postmaster General took charge of this department, as has been stated by Mr. Goddard in this letter, they had probably 10,000 such men as the postmaster at Poplar Point with whom they were in correspondence in order to make more active, if they possibly could, the Liberal organization in various parts of Canada. That is one of the great difficulties that the Postmaster General of that day had to contend with and I am glad to know that he was equal to the task they had placed in his hands, and that he was endeavouring to deal with such gentlemen as were being addressed by Mr. Goddard for the purpose of advancing the political views and organization of the Liberal party. Therefore, it is surprising to me to-night to find my hon. and innocent friend, the 171*	'
junior member for ] alifax, discussing political partisanship o i the part of the late Postmaster General.
Mr. A. K. MACLEAVi: The purpose of that circular would be to build up the post office revenues because the subscribers would have to send in their subscriptions. But my hon. friend was going to give me some proof. I do not consider that letter as proof.
It is the proof you asked for.

My hon. friend is not
serious in that.

The proof you asked for
was of political partisanship on the part of the late Government.	*

I would say that that
shows that Mr. Goddard was a partisan but not the postmaster.

I do not think he was
nearly as strong a partisan as the Postmaster General in the late Government with whom my hon. friend was associated.
If my hon. friend could show a partisan reply from the postmaster that would make his case good.

He evidently addressed
this letter to the wrong man. He was sending out 10,000 of them, but he evidently inside a mistake. He evidently sent 9,999 to the proper persons but he made one mistake and sent this circular to a Tory.
That just proves that lie is no partisan.

That proves the character of the organization that was in the Post Office Department previous to the present Government taking office. I am sure my hon. friend has very little to complain of if he makes a comparison of the administration between the two parties. We cannot appreciate too highly the energy, skill and unselfish devotion of my late colleague, Mr. Pelletier, in the performance of the great task that confronted him when he undertook the reorganization of the Post Office Department.

My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works is always humorous and to-night I really think he has excelled himself. He started out by saying that it was idle for us to accuse the present Postmaster General of partisanship and that the partisanship that existed in the department



under the late Administration had reached its highest point when Mr. Pelletier came into office as Postmaster General.
9 ,p.m. In support of that he read a letter which was sent out by the secretary of the association, Mr. Goddard, in which the request is made that certain literature will be distributed by postmasters throughout the various constituencies.
That is right.

The postmasters need not have done it unless they liked. There was nothing compulsory about it, but even tf they had been partisans to the extent of distributing the literature which had come into their offices, would there toe anything particularly harmful about that? It is a well known fact that both parties sent out literature to be distributed in all the constituencies in the Dominion, and in that respect one party is as guilty as the other, if such a word can be used in that connection. Both parties resort to those tactics in order to distribute their literature throughout Canada. To make the statement that no man had faced greater difficulties than the late Postmaster General when he took charge of the Post Office Department is to make a statement which appears to me to toe rather extraordinary. Why, Sir, in what way did he have any extraordinary difficulties to face? He came in with an overflowing treasury, he came in with everything working smoothly, and he came in with a most efficient staff. We find by reference to the reports of the Post Office Department that during the years beginning with 1902 and coming down to 1914, there were invariably surpluses in the department. In the year 1913 there was a surplus of $1,177,000. Then we see evidences of Mr. Pelletier's fine Italian hand; his policy begins to bear fruit, and in the year 1914 we find a surplus of only $134,157. But he only exhibited real statesmanship, he only showed how to run a department at the least possible expense, when he came down to 1915, because, in that year, although he had enhanced receipts from the sale of stamps, he had a deficit of $2,194,000. Surely the Minister of Public Works will not say that that deficit Was due to partisanship, to the maintenance of an organization in the Post Office Department toy the wicked Grits.
You had too many Liberal workers.	,

Between the year in which he took office and the year in which he had
[Mr. Pardee. 1
this great deficit, he had discharged thousands of Grit employees and taken on thousands of Tories; so that, surely, the Grit organization in the Post Office Department was being moderately weeded out. There were not as many good Grits left as there should have been, and yet, with that Tory organization, during the year 1915, this statesman managed to put this country into debt to the extent of $2,194,000. To convert a surplus of $1,174,000 into a deficit of $2,194,000 may toe statesmanship, but. it is the kind of statesmanship that I am not able to appreciate. I may not be able to define just what statesmanship is, tout if that is statesmanship,'I don't know what statesmanship is.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) says " hear, hear," and I take it he agrees with me that that is not the kind of statesmanship that should be entrusted with the administration of a public department. Perhaps it means that he is wholly in accord with the methods of the late Postmaster General, Mr. Pel-letiei.
I was expressing only approval of my hon. friend's statement that he did not know what statesmanship was.

May I re-echo my hon.
friend's " hear, hear," and say that he knows little about statesmanship. I was glad to hear the Postmaster General say to-night that in future-apparently he had not done it in the past, he intended to follow the practice of accepting the lowest tender; that whether the lowest tenderer was a Tory or Grit he would get the contract, and that the contract would not be peddled around until the lowest tenderer could be found amongst the friends of bis own party. That confession of faith, which I understood him to make to-night, is vastly different from the confession he made on the 22nd of March of this year, as reported on page 2105 of Hansard. On that occasion it was pointed out by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House that a Government was taking a very serious step when it departed from the system of tender and contract. If after calling for tenders, the system of awarding the contract to the lowest tenderer is not lived yp to, where is any party going to land itself? It simply means that the system of tender and contract is a subterfuge, an endeavour to pull the wool over the people's eyes. Nothing could be

more degrading than for a Government to advertise that the system of tender and contract shall prevail, and then, when the tenders have been put in, to say: " Here is a Grit tendering for $410; you, Tom Jones, are a good friend of the party, and the contract is yours if you put in a contract for $400/' I do not believe the Postmaster General has departed from the system of his own volition, but he must' admit that it is tampering with the public interest, and doing something that is not conducive to the best interests of any country or of any party. On page 2105 of Hansard the Postmaster General says:
I do not agree with my hon. friend that that is not fair, because no one could complain that the public interest suffers if the lowest tender is $500 and an opportunity is given to some one else to tender below that. My hon. friend says that is not fair. Well, I do not think so.
Then after a question by Mr. Marcil he
goes on:
If a tender has been sent in for $500, and information is received that the work can be done for $480, surely no one can complain that the public interest suffers, if, instead of the contract being, given to some one at $500, it is given to some one else at $480.
Now is it not as plain as anything could be that when the lowest tender is sent in by a man who is not a political friend of this party, the department says to its political friends in the conetituency concerned: John Jones, a Grit, has tendered for $500; if you, Sam Brown, who are a good Tory, send in a tender for $490, you will get the contract. That is simply throwing the system of tender and contract to the winds.
Does the Tory get the contract without fresh tenders being called for?

Yes, if we can take the Postmaster General's word; and I submit that the practice is pernicious in the extreme, and ought not to be followed again. If the system of tender and contract means anything, it means that the lowest tenderer, whether friend or foe of the party in power, shall be given the contract. Imagine any one arguing that preference is given be" cause one man can carry the rural mail better than his neighbour! Why, these men are all farmers and have horses and carts; they all know the roads, and, so far as being able to do the work goes, they 'are all as good as one another. That is no argument at all, it is simply an excuse. I submit that the Postmaster General should
in future stick to the strict letter of the law, and to what is morally right, and give the contract to the lowest tenderer.

Like a great many
other people in this country I have been at a loss to understand how it is that the disease of political corruption should have burst forth so suddenly, and with such extraordinary vigour. It is accounted for sometimes by excessive prosperity, sometimes by a luxury which begets wickedness, or by a lapse in morality, by faulty education, an ignorance of the moral law, or by disregard of the first principles of propriety and of the common precepts of every-day decent life. But if I am not mistaken, the Liberal party in Parliament at the present moment stands convicted of having condoned, in this letter, the most monstrous instance of political and moral obliquity that I have yet seen in this year of grace -or disgrace. This letter purports to be signed by the secretary of their political society, the president of which is the right hon. 'leader of the Opposition; and it purports to be addressed to the postmaster at Poplar Point.
Mr. A. K, MACLEAN: I am not in a position to deny that statement absolutely, but I think the document carries evidence on its face that it was not addressed to any postmaster. Down in the left-hand corner of the document you will see the letters "P. M. P. Point," not in the handwriting of Mr. Goddard, or of any one in his office, but of somebody else. It is very unlikely that it was distributed among the postmasters for that purpose. The . burden is on the Minister of Public Works to prove that the document was mailed to a postmaster. I do not believe it was myself.
I am sure it was.
It was an open circular, addressed to somebody not a postmaster.
It was addressed to the postmaster at Poplar Point.
It may have been inadvertently addressed to a man who happened to be a postmaster, but it was not deliberately addressed to a postmaster.

We need not have a herring drawn across the trail. A few moments ago, when the letter was thought to be authentic, and; it was understood that it had been written by Goddard, the secretary of the Liberal Association, to the postmas-

ter at Poplar Point, it was excused toy no less a man than the senior whip of the Liberal party (Mr. Pardee). The first man to attack its authenticity was the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). But he was too late; that objection should have been put in immediately.
I only just saw it.

You saw it too late.
The point is, the offence was condoned by hon. gentlemen opposite before they suggested that the document might not be authentic. Assuming that it was an authentic document, they proceeded to excuse it; and here we have the extraordinary fact that, at the very moment when they are teaching us a lesson in departmental regularity and morality in connection with the post office, we find them condoning such an offence as this, that this man can write to a man, who they supposed at the time to be a postmaster at Poplar Point, upbraiding him for not sending in a list of the active Liberal workers in the constituency, thus making of the postmaster a common political agent. How could he perform his duties; how could he be considered as the very flower of political morality or political decency, if the party known as the Liberal party, the apostles for the moment of purity, could excuse a letter like that through which the postmaster at an obscure town, and possibly the postmasters at thousands of other towns in Canada, are to be consecrated to the task of active political work, where the secret and sacred correspondence of the people is involved? I say there is no hope for the country-

Correspondence is not
sacred; it is all censored.

It is time for my hon. friends to interrupt; they have found out their blunder. They excuse it. If that is the condition of things in Canada, there is no need of holding investigations; we ought all to walk into the penitentiary.
Are you going now?

It is all very well to
laugh.

(Translation). Mr. Speaker, I should like to get some information from the Postmaster General regarding the system followed by his department in awarding contracts after tenders are called. I hold in my hands the return to an order of the House, made by the Post Office Department, in renly to my question
(Mr. Burnham.]
concerning the different tenders received and the different contracts awarded for the rural mail distribution in the counties of TAssomption and Montcalm. I find that in most cases the contract was not awarded to the lowest tenderer, but was given to another tenderer after he had been prevailed upon to alter his figures. Take, for instance, rural route No. 1 in the Laurentians. There were seven tenders, the lowest being $525 by Mr. Charles Gauthier. Mr. Charles Paquin had put in a tender for $595. The latter got the contract, after bringing his figures down to $550.
I have nothing to say against Mr. Paquin, but why should other tenderers be put aside and Mr. Paquin be allowed to alter his figures and be awarded the contracts
Route No. 3 in the Laurentians: Patrick Courtemauche had the lowest tender at $350. Mr. Edmond Therien had offered to take the contract at $500; yet the latter got the contract, after changing his tender to $345.
Saint-Roch de l'Achigan, route No 1: Three tenderers, J. W. Marien, $295. Mr. Roch Vezina asked $350. The latter was awarded the contract after he had been allowed to reduce his tender to $290.
Saint-Roch de l'Achigan, route No. 2: The lowest tenderer is Mr. Pierre Perrier. Mr. Henri Magnan's price was $690; but Mr. Magnan secured the job after he was allowed to alter his tender to $495.
Sault Saint-Lin: Lowest tenderer, Mr. Vincent Pelletier, $500. Mr. Omer Beriner had put in a tender at $595; the contract went to him after he had come down to $495.
Rawdon, route No. 1: Lowest tenderer, Mr. George Kirkwood, $335. Mr. G. E. Trudeau, whose first tender was for $500, was allowed to reduce his price to $330, and was given the contract.
Rawdon, rural route No. 2: Lowest tender, $390, from Mr. George Kirkwood. Mr. G. E. Trudeau put in a tender for $600. The latter was permitted to reduce his tender to $375 in order to secure the work.
I have no fault to find with those who were awarded the contracts; so much the better for them; but I wonder what principle was followed by the minister in thus discriminating in favour of certain tenderers, and in showing such preference without a care for justice.

I have often noticed that, when the House or the committee is seriously and earnestly discussing something that involves a question of principle,

the Minister of Public Works interrupts with irrelevant matter, and drags the discussion down to the plane of the ridiculous. He rose a few moments ago and said that the late Postmaster General was impeded in a fair administration of his department because he was surrounded 'by a great number of Liberal officials. I assume that when he refers to Liberal officials, he refers to officials of his department at Ottawa and in the leading postal centres of the Dominion, because it would hardly be correct to refer to country postmasters as officials of the department. In a sense they are officials, but I scarcely think the Minister of Public Works used the word in that sense. The only proof he produces of his assertion is a letter which was addressed to an unknown person, being a political circular from the Liberal headquarters at Ottawa, and which is unobjectionable in every respect. Somebody has written upon that circular the words "Postmaster, Poplar Point," and it is endorsed, I think, by the same hand on the back.
No, it is not.
Well, I cannot tell anything about it.
I can tell. I want to correct my hon. friend. That letter was addressed to the postmaster at Poplar Point, I take the responsibility for saying that.
I refer to the endorsa-tion on the back. I understand the Minister of Public Works to say that he received that document from the postmaster at Poplar Point.
I did not receive it from him, but I know it went to him.
You know it came from him; you could not know anything else. After all, is not that what my hon. friend means, that he got this document from the postmaster at Poplar Point?
I got the document; I have read it, and it speaks for itself. It is signed by Mr. Goddard.
And it came from the postmaster at Poplar Point? We are also informed by the Minister of Public Works that this postmaster is a Conservative.
I did not say so.
Yes, you did.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. You did say so. It is just as fair for me to say that that postmaster may have abstracted the letter from the box of the addressee at Poplar Point, knowing its contents, and for a little political pyrotechnics addressed it to his political leader the Minister of Public Works.
How could he know its contents?
There might be several ways. Postmasters know the contents of a great many things which go through their post offices.
Especially in country post offices.

Yes. Circulars are frequently opened in the post offices. That is just as rational a construction to put upon this little incident as the construction placed upon it by the Minister of Public Works. If I can prove that my construction is the correct one, the Conservative postmaster is guilty of a grave impropriety; but I thought the Minister of Public Works would be serious this evening in discussing this matter and not try to give a ridiculous turn to the whole thing by the production of some testimony which did not relate to the matter in any way whatever. The ground he takes, that the late Postmaster General was surrounded by partisan officials appointed by the late Government, is a serious statement to make, if he really meant it. I do not know whether the Minister of Public Works really meant what he said. I would say that had the late Postmaster General permitted the officials of his department to administer that department as they had been accustomed to under the Liberal Postmaster General, the department would never have got into the condition which it so quickly got into while the late Postmaster General was responsible for its administration. I wonder if the Minister of -Public Works has any greater respect for the system of contract than has the Post Office Department. Does the minister's department respect the system of tender and contract?
Always.
Does he permit any one to put in a tender after the tenders have been opened and the lowest disclosed?

Never.
Mr. MACLEANj What would the Minister of Public Works think of what the Post-

master General said the other night? 1 refer to page 2105 of Hansard. The discussion will appear from the statement I shall read:
Mr. Casgrain: I do not agree with my hon. friend that that is not fair, because no one could complain that the public interest suffers if the lowest tender is $500 and'an opportunity is given to some one else to tender below that. My hon. friend says that is not fair. Well, I do not think so.
The Postmaster General is thus on record as having stated that after tenders have been received;, and it is known who is the lowest tenderer and the amount of his tender, it is perfectly right to receive secretly tenders below that figure. Will the Minister of Pulblic Works tell me if he approves of that?
That is your side of the story.

No, I am giving your
side of the story as related by the Postmaster General; and what the Postmaster General describes is what we are objecting to. I have never saicl a word about mail contracts being given to Conservatives. That occasions a good deal of discontent in rural communities; but after all it is not a serious matter who carries the mail, so long as the system of tender and contract is respected. I have put a question to the Minister of Public Works, a fair one; there is no disagreement as to the facts; and I would like him to answer the question. He says he would not do this in his own department. Will he tell us just what he thinks of the same thing when it is done in the Post Office Department?

The Postmaster General
will tell you.

No, no, no. I am asking the question of the Minister of Public Works, who was so brave in attempting to prove something a few moments ago, but signally failed because he was talking of something that had no bearing on the subject before the committee.

I would like to know
wherein I failed.

We will drop that for
the moment. I want him to say what he thinks of that statement of the Postmaster General. He came into this discussion un; invited, and unless he can contribute something
I think I have the same right to come into the discussion as my hon. friend has.

I think I should
shoulder my own sins; I do not see why my hon. friend (Mr. Rogers) should shoulder my sins if I have any. I do not think the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) , was quite fair when he said I absolutely approved of the system by which, after tenders were asked for, any one could come in and put in a lower bid and get the contract. If hon. members will refer to page 2106, they will see that I said, " I do not think the public interest has suffered." The whole question was whether the public interest had suffered in the particular instance which we were discussing. Let me recall to the minds of hon. members how the system of tender and contract works in the Post Office Department since I have had charge of it. We are obliged to ask tenders for any mail contracts above $200, and I may say that we always have a great many tenderers. It is naturally necessary for us to ask somebody acquainted with the parties in the constituency whether the tenderer is a fit and proper person to carry the mail.
Do not you ask for bonds for the successful tenderer?
Yes.
Does not that speak for itself?
No, and I will tell my hon. friend why. Tenders are put in, in many cases, by minors, who cannot, according to the law of the province of Quebec, bind themselves.
Do not the bondsmen protect you?

The contractor has to be a person capable of performing the work and assuming the obligations of the contract. In many instances, to my own knowledge, men have tendered and have given security, who are, for instance, drunkards, and not qualified or able to carry out the contracts in question. That is the reason why information is asked for. And, so far as I am concerned, I never knew what the politics of the tenderer was. My principle is that the contract must be given to the lowest tenderer irrespective of any party preference. In many cases, especially in the carrying of rural mail-

and, so far as I can tell, that must have been the case in the matters referred to by my hon. friend from L'Assomption (Mr. Seguin)-even the lowest tenderer is above the price fixed by the department for the work. The maximum which is given is $30 a mile, and in every case in which this amount is exceeded-or in some cases at least-the contract is given to some of those who have tendered and who will come down to the price set by the department, and which was lower than that of the lowest tenderer.
In that case, would not you think that the lowest tenderer should be asked first whether he could come down?
I have not a personal knowledge of the case cited.

(Translation.) Mir. Chairman, I admit that in most cases the contracts were awarded at five dollars less than the price stated in the lowest tender; but it seems certain to me that had the lowest tenderer been offered the chance to lower his tender by five dollars, he would have found it easier to do so than some of the other tenderers who, to reach the five-dollar-less mark, had to cut down their original tender $100 or more.

The statement of the
minister is, that in some cases he would make inquiry as to the character and suitability of the lowest tenderer. In such cases, would he inquire of Liberals or of Conservatives in the locality?

I think the hon. member is pushing the matter a little too far. If I have a man in whom I have confidence, I do not see why I should inquire whether that man is a Liberal or a Conservative, when I seek to gain through him information as to any given person who wishes to make a contract with the department. But I say quite frankly that if I have a political friend in the constituency, I would rather ask him.

In every case, the hon. gentleman would naturally do so. In country districts there is usually very strong political feeling, and in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, a political friend of the Government would feel himself quite justified in reporting that the lowest tenderer, if a Liberal, would not be quite so suitable as a Conservative who might be willing to take it. The difficulty I see about the matter is that
the minister has laid down an entirely unjustifiable principle, upon which he felt justified in acting. He admits that in the case referred to he called for tenders, and then passed over the lowest tenderer and allowed some other party to take the contract at a few dollars less than the amount of the lowest tender. That seems entirely wrong. If it could properly be done in the Department of the Postmaster General it could be done with equal propriety in the Department of Public Works, and I am sure the Minister of Public Works will agree at once that it would be entirely contrary to the proper administration of affairs for him as minister to act in that way. I know that during the whole time I was Minister of Public Works I never permitted such a thing to foe done; it would have been absolutely improper; it would not have been permitted by my colleagues in council, even if I had suggested it to them.
Does my hon. friend say he never did that?
Never did that, never once.
If my hon. friend asked for tenders for a work the estimated cost of which was $10,000, and received a tender for $50,000, that being the lowest tender, would he give the contract to that man?
Not at all. I would call for new tenders.
Was it not the case .frequently when he was minister that he refused to receive the lowest tender because it was too high?
Yes, I have done that; but I have invariably-
A moment ago you said you never did it.
I never said anything of the kind; the hon. member must be deaf not only in one ear, but in both.
My hon. friend said he always accepted the lowest tender and never departed from that principle.
Never.
The principle the Postmaster General referred to was where the tenders were on rural routes, and the limit was $30 a mile.

The hon. member does
not try to understand what I say. My statement was that it was exceedingly improper;

that I was sure the Minister of Public Works felt it would be improper; that when I was minister I never did such a thing, and that I would consider it exceedingly improper, and I was sure my colleagues would not have, tolerated for a single moment that I should pass over the lowest tenderer and pick out somebody else and give him the contract. It is a very different thing to call for new tenders. I have done that very often. Where the lowest tenderer was reported to me by the engineers in my department as being too high, I have called for new tenders; and in some cases where the lowest tender had been considered too high I have offered the contract to the lowest tenderer if he would take it for smaller amount; but never did I deem it proper, never did I deem it right, that I should ask my colleagues or Parliament to permit me to pass over the lowest tenderer and give the contract to somebody else. If that is not proper in the Department of Public Works, it is not proper in the Department of the Postmaster General. But the Postmaster General argued that the country did not lose anything, but, on the contrary, saved $20. So it would be in the Public Works Department. If a minister called for tenders and half a dozen tenders came in and the lowest tender was for $10,000, then if the minister could say to a friend who was not the lowest tenderer: Now, if you will do this for $9,950, I will pass over the lowest tenderer and give the contract to you, the public interest would not suffer, because $50 would be saved. But it is an absolutely wrong principle, and something not only contrary to justice and fair play, but contrary to the meaning of the statute which declares that tenders shall be called for. The minister says that sometimes it might occur that the lowest tenderer would be a drunkard, would be incapable of performing the work. Then he would be justified in passing over the lowest tenderer and taking the next one. If a man was not qualified, if he had been unsatisfactory in the performance of a previous contract, that might be done; but in this particular case there was nothing in the world against the lowest tenderer. The minister did not give it to the other party on the ground that the lowest tenderer was not a good man, but apparently gave it to a political friend, who chose to do the work for a few dollars less than the amount of the lowest tender. I am sure that, on reflection, the Postmaster General will admit that that is entirely unfair.

Take a private individual-and surely the administration of public affairs ought to be governed by principles as high as a private individual would feel himself to be governed by-the ordinary man who wants work done invites people to tender, to make offers to him of the lowest prices at which they will do the work. There is an implied contract, an implied obligation, on the part of the man calling for those tenders, that he will award the contract to the lowest tenderer, provided his price is fair and reasonable. If it is not he will call for tenders again, or offer the contract to the lowest tenderer if he will reduce his price. But to go through the farce of calling for tenders simply to enable him to give the contract to a political friend, or to some friend whether political or otherwise, at a slightly lower price than that of the lowest tender, is entirely wrong. When men tender they go to a certain amount of work; they figure up with care what they can do the work fox, they arrange for their bondsmen, and put in a tender, having a right to believe that they will foe treated fairly, and that the lowest tender will be accepted. Then the minister says it is right to ignore altogether his public call for tenders, to ignore altogether any obligation he is under to the man who has gone to trouble and expense and has put in his tender to the department. He says that he is entirely justified in picking out a political friend and giving the contract to him for a few dollars less than the amount of the lowest tender. I am sure that is a view which will not commend itself to any member on either side of thi^ House.

The point raised by the member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) seems to be a very important one for the committee to consider. The Postmaster General the other day said that he believed in the system that has been followed; he believed it was perfectly proper, after the tenders had been received, to communicate with gentlemen who had tendered, and if they were in a position to reduce their tender to a certain amount, a few dollars or cents less than the lowest tender, to give them the contract. I am sure from the statements made by my hon. friend to-night that he has changed his mind in regard to that being a proper system of letting mail contracts in his department. I wish to cite to my hon. friend an instance which bears out exactly what the hon. member for Halifax was

arguing during this discussion. Down in my province a short time ago, I think about the time when the public were calling in tones louder than thunder for an election, it was proposed to inaugurate a rural mail route in a certain portion of the province. When they started to inaugurate this new rural route, a gentleman came to my office, a man who had been maimed in one hand and was not able to work. He wanted to get this contract. He had the form of tender and wanted me to show him how to fill it out. I said:	"Sit down and I will
fill it out and you can sign it right here." He said: " I do not want to sign it, I only want to find out how to make this tender." I said, "What do you want to do about it?" Hie reply wias that he had been to see the dispenser of patronage. My hon. friend the Postmaster General would have this committee believe that politics are not taken into consideration in the letting of contracts for the carrying of mails, but that man said: "I have seen the dispenser of patronage in. the county where I live, and he says it will not do for me to put in a tender, because I am not on the right side of politics." He was not allowed to tender at all, and a strong Conservative in the locality, who did not have a horse, or a vehicle of iany kind put in a tender in his own name and sub-let it to the man who is doing the driving to-day.
Will my hon. friend give me the man's name?

I will give it to my hon. friend privately. The man consulted me in private, and I would not like to make his name public. That is what took place. If my hon. friend and his predecessor did not take politics into consideration in letting those contracts at any rate the dispensers of patronage in different localities look after the political end of matters, and my hon. friend is being deceived by these dispensers of patronage, at all events, by the dispenser in the locality I have mentioned. I merely cite this case in support of the argument of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) that the principle adopted by the Postmaster General is wrong, and that a man who is the lowest tenderer should not have to go to the dispenser of patronage or to any other1 person. If he puts in a tender and names his bondsman, and his is the lowest tender, he should get the contract, and he should not have to go to any dispenser of patronage
to get a recommendation on the strength of his politics.
How long has my hon. friend held that view?
I have always held that view, and, so far as I have had anything to do with patronage, I have always followed that principle.
For how long has my hon. friend expressed that view?

On the motion of Mr. Rogers for the adjournment of the House:
What business will be taken to-morrow?

I would draw the attention of my hon. friend to the fact, which he very well knows, that we have been in session now for three months or over, and we have all worked pretty hard. We had a certain understanding, at all events, it was hoped that we would prorogue at Easter. I am satisfied, if hon. gentlemen are willing to be diligent, and to facilitate the balance of the business that has to be brought down to the House, that that is still possible. I am sure that a great number of hon. members on both sides of the House are very anxious to get away. I hear that desire expressed every day; it is,common to members on both sides of the House. So far as the Government is concerned, we are willing to facilitate the business in every possible way, either by having morning sessions, or in any other way that will be convenient to members, in the hope of reaching prorogation, if not before Easter a very few days later.
Is there any new business to be brought down?
There is nothing new other than what the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition has had notice of.

There is a rumour that there is to be same railway legislation of an important character, but the Prime Minister has not, so far as I knpw, announced it to the House. If the Minister of Public Works will say there is to be no such legislation, we will be glad to hear it.

I am not in a position to say. I understand that the Prime Minister and the right hon. leader of the Opposition have discussed in detail the legislation that is to be brought down, and if my hon. friend wants information along that line, I am satisfied he can get it from his leader. I sincerely hope that hon. gentlemen will be willing to facilitate the business of the House, in the hope that we will be able to reach prorogation at an early date.

In reply to my hon. friend I may point out that there was a notice of motion on the Order Paper to-day, that on and after Wednesday next morning sessions would be held, but, when that notice of motion was reached, the Prime Minister asked that it be allowed to stand, which was notice to the House that the Government did not think it possible to prorogue before Easter. I do not know whether it is possible or not; my judgment would be that, in consideration of the business yet before the House, and in view of what has taken place, and of what is likely to take place, it is improbable that prorogation could take place before Easter. In fact, it was rumoured in the corridors to-day that the Government was considering a proposal that the House adjourn on Friday next and stand adjourned until the Tuesday following Easter. I would ask my hon. friend if that is the decision which the Government have arrived at- Another question I wculd like to ask is: would it mot be wise to postpone even adjournment for the Easter recess until the Minister of Militia has been given an opportunity to make a statement before the House. I think it is his right to do so, as it is our duty to allow him that privilege. If there is to be a lengthy adjournment at Easter, it is hardly fair that the minister should not be given that opportunity, after all that has been allowed to go on Hansard.
The question raised by my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) is very important. I have not had any information that there was to be legislation brought down as coming from the right hon. the Prime Minister or any member of the Government, although I am not saying that it has not been given to my

right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. It is rumoured, however, that the Quebec and Saguenay railway expect to get aid of some kind and details of that aid have been given in certain places, s* that the matter must have been discussed at considerable length by the Government. There is also a very lively rumour that a Bill is now being prepared granting certain aid to the Canadian Northern Railway Company. If that be true the Government ought to give the House its programme. It has also been stated that legislation is to be brought down in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific. I do not know whether these things are true or not-the Government know-but if these large measures are to be brought down they will certainly cause considerable discussion, and that being the case, I think the Minister of Public Works can hardly be serious in thinking that they can be jammed through before Easter.
I am sure that the Government have no desire to jam through any legislation.

I do not think there is
any possible chance of an adjournment for any extended period at Easter, unless there is a prospect of getting the business closed at a very early date, because hon. members who are here and who come from a distance, are most anxious to remain at their work until the business of the House has been completed.
In respect to my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes), I believe, from information I have, that he will probably be in his seat on Friday of this week. If the boat on which he sailed makes its usual connections the minister will be here on Friday and I am sure that he will be prepared and willing to answer anything that he may be called upon to answer as to the administration of his department. With respect to legislation, an announcement will be made almost immediately by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister as to what additional legislation is to be brought down, and I am sure that it will not be of such an important character that it would not be possible for this House to give it all the consideration that was necessary and even then, if we were diligent in our efforts, be able to prorogue Parliament o* Thursday night before Easter Sunday. However, if that is impossible, we will have to keep on and in that case it will not be possible to have an extended adjournment during the Easter holidays.
